Build small guards. Compose them.

is-kit is a lightweight, zero-dependency toolkit for building reusable TypeScript type guards.

is-kit is not just a collection of isX helpers. Its main focus is composing small runtime checks into reusable guards while preserving useful TypeScript narrowing.

It helps you write small isFoo functions, compose them into richer runtime checks, refine properties on values you already know about, and keep TypeScript narrowing natural inside regular control flow. Use it at runtime boundaries when needed, without requiring a schema-first workflow.

Runtime-safe 🛡️, composable 🧩, and ergonomic ✨ without asking you to adopt a heavy schema workflow.

  • Build and reuse typed guards
  • Compose guards with and, or, not, oneOf
  • Use refineKey to narrow a child property while preserving its parent type
  • Validate object shapes and collections when that is useful
  • Parse or assert unknown values without a large schema framework

Best…

View on GitHub

If it looks useful, a ⭐ on GitHub is always very welcome!

Thanks for reading! 🙌

articles.title: My OSS Projects: Picard.js
articles.description: This is part of my series "My Open-Source Projects", where I walk through the projects I started or...
articles.body_html:
This is part of my series "My Open-Source Projects", where I walk through the projects I started or helped to grow – with the back story, what they do well, where they struggle, and what's next. Previous parts: AngleSharp, MAGES, Piral, Electron.NET and Netpack.

Today's project is the one that is simultaneously my youngest and the one that comes with the biggest "well, actually" disclaimer: Picard.js. It is a micro frontend orchestrator – a small library that can bring micro frontends to any page, no matter how that page was built.

Before you ask: yes, the name is a Star Trek reference. No, I will not stop making "Make it so" jokes. Engage.

What is Picard.js?

Picard.js is a lightweight, flexible variant of the ideas behind Piral. It combines multiple micro frontend technologies – pilets, Module Federation, Native Federation, and more – behind one small, uniform surface. The important bit: you do not need a Piral instance, and you do not need a Native Federation shell, to use it.

The official tagline is "The Captain for Shipping the Next Generation of Micro Frontends Federation and Beyond". The docs also say something I like a lot: Picard is an extension rather than a replacement for the technologies it works with.

In practice that means:

  • You have an existing app – an old PHP site, a static site, an ASP.NET page, a server-rendered thing from 2012 that nobody dares to touch.
  • You add one script tag.
  • You use custom elements such as <pi-component> and <pi-slot> to say where micro frontends should show up.
  • Picard loads them (from whatever format they come in), renders them, and keeps the page alive even if one of them explodes.

That's it. No new build, no new shell, no migration project that needs a steering committee.

How it came to be

If you read the Piral article, you know the deal: Piral is a full framework for micro frontends. App shell, CLI, ecosystem, the works. And very good at it. But a full framework is a full commitment – and not every project can, or wants to, commit.

Over the years the same questions kept coming up:

  • "Can I use this in my existing app without turning it into a Piral app?"
  • "Can I mix pilets with Module Federation?"
  • "Can I just load a micro frontend into a plain HTML page?"

The honest answer was always "sort of, but…". Picard is the "yes" to those questions.

The initial version was outlined at the Micro Frontends Conference in June 2024, where it was revealed in the closing keynote, "Painless Micro Frontend Orchestration with Picard". The pitch back then was: one library to just embed micro frontends – no tooling required, no constraints implied. In your existing web app, in a mobile app, or even in an Electron shell.

The first releases followed quickly in July 2024. And then… things got quiet. Development was paused in 2025 for a while. Life, other projects (hello, Netpack), and the small matter of figuring out what the future of Piral should look like.

That last point is actually the interesting one, because the pause had a purpose.

Picard is the foundation of Piral v2

There is now a clear roadmap for Piral v2, and it is built on top of Picard. The FAQ puts it precisely: Picard is not Piral's successor – it is the base library for Piral v2, effectively replacing piral-base.

So the relationship is:

  • Piral = the full framework (shell, tooling, ecosystem, opinions)
  • Picard = the engine that loads and renders micro frontends (few opinions, many formats)

The most important difference when you pick one: Piral always requires a micro frontend discovery server (a pattern Piral popularized), while Picard treats it as optional. With Picard you can point at a discovery service, hand it a list, give it a function – or simply reference a micro frontend by URL right in the markup.

The Piral v2 plan also gives us a nice tie-in with the Electron.NET article: the presets in the tracking issue are spa, ssr, islands, electron, tauri and react-native. One foundation, many runtimes.

Getting started

The one-liner 

<script src="https://unpkg.com/picard-js"></script>

Drop that into a page (or use jsDelivr, or install it from npm as picard-js) and the custom elements start working. If you have a discovery service, add its URL via the feed attribute on the script tag:

<script src="https://unpkg.com/picard-js" feed="https://feed.example.com/api/v1/pilet"></script>

Rendering a component

The workhorse is <pi-component>. You tell it what to render and where it comes from:

<!-- a Module Federation micro frontend -->
<pi-component
  name="product-teaser"
  source="https://shop.example.com/mf-manifest.json"
  format="module">
</pi-component>

<!-- a Native Federation micro frontend -->
<pi-component
  name="checkout-button"
  source="https://checkout.example.com/remoteEntry.json"
  format="native">
</pi-component>

<!-- a pilet -->
<pi-component
  name="newsletter"
  source="https://cdn.example.com/newsletter/index.meta.json"
  format="pilet">
</pi-component>

Other attributes you will meet along the way include remote-name and remote-type (var or esm) for Module Federation, framework (e.g. single-spa), loading-template-id for a loading placeholder, and client (e.g. visible) to control when it gets activated.

Rendering everything that matches

<pi-slot> is the sibling for the "extension slot" idea you may know from Piral: it renders all components registered under a name – from all loaded micro frontends.

<ul>
  <pi-slot name="menu-item" item-template-id="menu-entry"></pi-slot>
</ul>

<template id="menu-entry">
  <li><slot></slot></li>
</template>

Teams can add menu entries without anyone touching the host page. (Slots also support ordering via attributes.)

Using it from code

Not everything has to be markup. The client variant is a regular module:

import { initializePicard } from 'picard-js/client';

initializePicard({
  feed: 'https://feed.example.com/api/v1/pilet',
});

feed is flexible: a URL string, an array of pilet metadata, a discovery response (Piral Feed Service or the MFE working group schema), a map of Native Federation manifests – or a function returning a promise of any of those.

The generic lifecycle

How does Picard render a component written in React, Vue, Svelte or "something my colleague wrote at 2 am"? Via a small, generic lifecycle:

A component exposes some or all of these. A minimal sketch with React looks like this:

import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';
import { Teaser } from './Teaser';

export default {
  mount(container, props) {
    const root = createRoot(container);
    root.render(<Teaser {...props} />);
    container.__root = root;
  },
  update(container, props) {
    container.__root.render(<Teaser {...props} />);
  },
  unmount(container) {
    container.__root.unmount();
  },
};

If you already have single-spa parcels, there is an adapter for those too (framework="single-spa", client only). So you are not forced to rewrite anything to be "Picard compatible".

Errors stay contained

One thing I care about a lot: a micro frontend that fails to load, or crashes while rendering, must not take the page with it. Picard handles bad references and crashing components gracefully. (For debugging, the Piral Inspector works with Picard, too.)

Server-side rendering and islands

Because Picard is "just" a library with a Node variant, it is not restricted to client-side pages.

  • The node variant (picard-js/node) takes your HTML, finds the pi-component elements, and replaces them with their server-rendered output (via the stringify step of the lifecycle) plus the state the browser needs. There is also the pi-part element – a server-only replacement rule – which, for example, injects the display: contents styling for the custom elements.
  • The islands variant is a lightweight resumption approach: the page already looks right, the interactive script loads after first paint, and components hydrate only where needed (hydrate attribute, or detected in mount by a non-empty container).

The repository's examples cover static pages (with and without a feed, with routing, with single-spa), an SSR example, an islands example, and dependency sharing. And on the server examples we keep a self-imposed rule: they have to reach a Lighthouse score of 100. It's a good constraint to have when your whole purpose is being lightweight.

Where Picard shines

  • Brownfield-friendly. One script tag and some custom elements. Your PHP page doesn't need to know what a bundler is.
  • Format-agnostic. Pilets, Module Federation (v1 and v2), Native Federation and plain native ES modules – side by side, on the same page.
  • Small. The upcoming 0.3.0 reduces the browser script from 106 kB to 33 kB (the Module Federation runtime is loaded on demand), and the interactive script loads after the first paint.
  • Optional discovery. Works great with a discovery server, doesn't require one.
  • Resilient. Broken micro frontends don't break the page.
  • Framework-agnostic. If it can map to the lifecycle, it can be rendered.

Where it struggles (the honest part)

Let's be adults about this:

  • It is an early preview. The changelog says "Early preview: Not suitable for production yet" on every entry. I mean that.
  • The published version is old. The latest release on npm is 0.2.3 from July 2024. The docs already describe 0.3.0, which is still unreleased and lives in develop. (Yes, the docs are ahead of the package. I know.)
  • The docs are thin in places. The Electron page is a placeholder, and the FAQ still has "feature complete by end of July 2024" and "production ready in September 2024". Those dates are… let's call them aspirational. They are on my list for the finalization.
  • Small community. ~49 GitHub stars and a few dozen weekly downloads. Picard is not widely adopted – yet. If you need something battle-tested today, use Piral.
  • Not a framework. There is no CLI that scaffolds your world. That's by design, but it also means more is on you.

Community and licensing

The code is MIT licensed. Questions and discussions happen in the Piral community Discord, and issues and PRs on GitHub are very welcome – especially for the examples and docs.

Contributing is lighter than it sounds: the project uses esbuild for the examples, Playwright for tests (Node 22+), and preview releases (-pre.N) are published straight from develop.

What's next

The roadmap is refreshingly short:

  1. Finalize Picard v1. Settle the API, finish the docs, remove the "early preview" banner. It will ship toward the end of this year (2026).
  2. Piral v2 on top of it, with the presets spa, ssr, islands, electron, tauri and react-native.
  3. More examples and guides – and more FAQ items.

If you have a use case that Picard should handle, please open an issue. This is the right moment to shape it.

Links

  • 🌐 Website: picard.js.org
  • 📖 Docs: picard.js.org/guide
  • 💻 GitHub: picardjs/picard
  • 📦 npm: picard-js

Previous articles in this series:

  • AngleSharp
  • MAGES
  • Piral
  • Electron.NET
  • Netpack

Next up in this series

There are still a few projects waiting in the hangar. Stay tuned – and until then: make it so.

articles.title: Zone.js Hijacked Your Browser for 8 Years. Here's What Replaced It.
articles.description: A visual deep dive into how Angular tore out global browser monkey-patching and rebuilt its reactivity engine from scratch using Signals and Zoneless change detection.
articles.body_html:
Every frontend framework has to solve the same foundational challenge: when data changes in memory, how does the framework know which pixels on the screen need updating?

React chose virtual DOM diffing. Svelte chose compile-time DOM mutations.

For nearly ten years, Angular had the strangest answer in modern web development: it hijacked your entire browser.

If you called setTimeout, Angular intercepted it. If you clicked a button, Angular hijacked addEventListener. If you fetched data over the network, Angular wrapped fetch and XMLHttpRequest.

The library doing this heavy lifting was called Zone.js. It did not actually know what data changed, or which component owned that data. It only knew one blunt fact: an asynchronous browser API had finished running.

Because something might have changed, Angular did the only thing it could: it walked down your entire component tree, checking every single binding from top to bottom.

Over the last few versions, the Angular team quietly pulled off one of the most audacious architectural rewiring jobs in frontend history. They removed the monkey-patches, dismantled the global tree scans, and rebuilt Angular around Signals and Zoneless change detection.

To write modern, high-performance Angular, you have to understand how the old trick worked, why it ran out of road, and how the new reactive engine actually updates your DOM today.

The Zone.js Era: The Illusion of Automatic Reactivity

To understand where Angular is today, we have to look at what Zone.js was actually doing behind the scenes.

Consider this classic Angular component:

@Component({
  selector: 'app-counter',
  template: `
    <button (click)="increment()">Clicks: {{ count }}</button>
  `
})
export class CounterComponent {
  count = 0;

  increment() {
    this.count++;
  }
}

Notice what is missing here:

  • No setState() call like in React.
  • No this.triggerUpdate() call.
  • Just a plain property mutation: this.count++.

How did Angular know that this.count changed from 0 to 1?

The surprising answer is: it didn't.

Angular had no idea that count was touched. Instead, when your application booted up, Zone.js replaced the browser's native addEventListener with a patched wrapper.

When the user clicked the button, the execution pipeline went like this:

  1. The browser fired the native click event.
  2. Zone.js intercepted the callback.
  3. Your increment() function ran and mutated this.count.
  4. Zone.js detected that the microtask queue was empty (onMicrotaskEmpty).
  5. Zone.js notified Angular: "An async task just completed."
  6. Angular executed ApplicationRef.tick().
  7. Angular started at the very top of your application (the Root Component) and traversed every active child component, evaluating every template expression to see if any value differed from the previous cycle. 
       User Action (Click / Timer / Network Fetch)
                           │
                           ▼
          Browser Native API Intercepted by Zone.js
                           │
                           ▼
              Component Handler Executes
              (count++ in component memory)
                           │
                           ▼
          Zone.js Microtask Queue Becomes Empty
                           │
                           ▼
              Notify Angular: onMicrotaskEmpty
                           │
                           ▼
               ApplicationRef.tick()
                           │
        ┌──────────────────┴──────────────────┐
        ▼                                     ▼
   Root Component                     Component Tree Walk
   (Check bindings)                 (Check every child node)

This model was convenient, but it was an architectural blunt instrument.

If you had a dashboard with 2,000 components and a setInterval ticking in a background widget, Angular could end up checking thousands of template expressions every second, even if 99% of those components were completely static.

Why OnPush Was Only a Partial Cure

To stop these wasteful global tree traversals, Angular introduced ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush.

When you marked a component as OnPush, you gave Angular permission to skip that component's subtree during a change detection cycle, unless one of a few specific conditions was met:

  1. One of the component's @Input() references changed to a new memory address.
  2. An event listener declared directly inside that component's template was triggered.
  3. An AsyncPipe in the template emitted a new value.
  4. You manually injected ChangeDetectorRef and called markForCheck().

OnPush delivered enormous performance boosts, but it shifted mental overhead onto the developer. Mutating an object property in place broke change detection because the object reference remained unchanged.

Developers spent years debugging "ghost states", situations where component properties held fresh data, but the screen refused to re-render because no input reference had swapped.

The New Foundation: Signals and the Dependency Graph

Modern Angular replaces the global guessing game with a fine-grained reactive dependency graph powered by Signals.

A Signal is not an event stream, and it is not an RxJS Subject. A Signal is a synchronous reactive value wrapper that implements a two-way contract between Producers and Consumers.

import { signal, computed } from '@angular/core';

// Producer: holds a value and tracks who is listening
const count = signal(0);
const multiplier = signal(2);

// Producer & Consumer: listens to dependencies, produces a new value
const total = computed(() => count() * multiplier());

Here is what happens inside the runtime when this code runs:

  1. When computed() evaluates its formula, it temporarily registers itself as the active consumer on the global execution stack.
  2. Calling count() reads the current number, but it also registers an invisible edge in the dependency graph: total depends on count.
  3. Calling multiplier() registers another edge: total depends on multiplier.
  4. The graph is now wired.

When you update a signal via count.set(5), Angular does not re-run every calculation immediately.

Instead, it uses a push-pull algorithm:

  • Push notification: The changed signal pushes a lightweight "dirty" flag down the dependency graph to all consumers.
  • Pull evaluation: The consumer only recalculates its value when someone actually reads it.

If a computed signal is never read by an active template, it does not do the calculation work. This guarantees that your application never spends CPU cycles computing state that nobody is looking at.

Going Zoneless: How Angular Knows to Refresh the Screen

With Signals in place, modern Angular takes the decisive next step: eliminating Zone.js entirely.

You can configure an Angular application to run in Zoneless mode with a single provider:

// app.config.ts
import { ApplicationConfig, provideExperimentalZonelessChangeDetection } from '@angular/core';

export const appConfig: ApplicationConfig = {
  providers: [
    provideExperimentalZonelessChangeDetection()
  ]
};

When you turn off Zone.js, the monkey-patches disappear. Angular stops intercepting setTimeout, fetch, and native DOM events.

Without Zone.js waking up Angular, how does the framework know when to update the DOM?

Modern Angular introduces the ChangeDetectionScheduler. Instead of listening to global browser events, the scheduler only wakes up when it receives an explicit notification from one of five distinct sources:

  1. A Signal read in a template updates its value: When a template reads {{ user() }}, the template's view becomes a reactive consumer. Calling user.set(newProfile) flags that view dirty.
  2. A template event listener fires: When a user clicks <button (click)="save()">, Angular's template binding triggers the scheduler.
  3. An AsyncPipe emits: The pipe explicitly schedules a render check when new data arrives.
  4. An input changes: Calling ComponentRef.setInput() notifies the scheduler.
  5. Manual notification: An explicit call to ChangeDetectorRef.markForCheck().

When any of these triggers fire, the ChangeDetectionScheduler batches the requests into a single microtask using the browser's native queueMicrotask.

Even if your code updates fifty signals across three services in the same synchronous execution block, Angular only runs change detection once on the next microtask tick.

And when it runs, it checks only the components and views that were marked dirty by the reactive graph. Unaffected parts of the tree are completely skipped.

Seeing the Difference: A Real Code Walkthrough

Let us look at how this changes everyday component code.

Here is a modern, Zoneless-ready Angular component:

import { Component, signal, computed } from '@angular/core';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-order-summary',
  standalone: true,
  template: `
    <div class="card">
      <h2>Order Total: ${{ total() }}</h2>
      <p>Items in cart: {{ itemCount() }}</p>

      <button (click)="addItem(25)">Add $25 Item</button>
      <button (click)="clearCart()">Reset</button>
    </div>
  `
})
export class OrderSummaryComponent {
  // Writable Signals
  private prices = signal<number[]>([10, 20]);

  // Derived Computed Signal
  itemCount = computed(() => this.prices().length);
  total = computed(() => this.prices().reduce((sum, p) => sum + p, 0));

  addItem(price: number) {
    this.prices.update(items => [...items, price]);
  }

  clearCart() {
    this.prices.set([]);
  }
}

What makes this component fundamentally different from older Angular versions?

First, there are no lifecycle hacks. You do not need ngOnChanges or manual subscriptions to calculate derived totals. If prices changes, total and itemCount update their dependencies automatically.

Second, in a Zoneless setup, clicking the button does not trigger a global audit of other unrelated components across your app.

The update to prices marks the template view of OrderSummaryComponent as dirty. The scheduler coalesces the update, visits this single component during the microtask, and patches the two interpolation text nodes directly.

Three Traps to Avoid When Moving to Zoneless

As teams migrate their codebases toward Zoneless Angular, three common pitfalls tend to surface:

Trap 1: Mutating Plain Class Properties

In the old Zone.js world, this code worked because Zone.js caught the click event and checked everything anyway:

// ❌ Old habit that breaks in Zoneless
export class ProfileComponent {
  userName = 'Sarah';

  updateName() {
    this.userName = 'Alex'; // Screen will NOT update if triggered outside template events!
  }
}

If updateName() is called from a WebSocket event, an RxJS stream, or a native callback, Angular has no way of knowing this.userName changed.

The Fix: Wrap mutable view state in a Signal:

// ✅ Zoneless-safe
export class ProfileComponent {
  userName = signal('Sarah');

  updateName() {
    this.userName.set('Alex');
  }
}

Trap 2: Unintended Signal Tracking Inside Effects

Angular provides effect() for running side effects when signals change (such as logging or syncing to local storage).

effect(() => {
  console.log(`Current user: ${this.currentUser()}`);
  // If you also read another signal here for logging...
  console.log(`Analytics ID: ${this.analyticsId()}`);
});

Because effect() tracks every signal read within its callback, this effect will re-run whenever currentUser changes, but also whenever analyticsId changes.

The Fix: Use untracked() when you only want to read a secondary signal without subscribing to it:

import { effect, untracked } from '@angular/core';

effect(() => {
  const user = this.currentUser();
  const id = untracked(() => this.analyticsId());

  console.log(`User ${user} logged with ID ${id}`);
});

Trap 3: Subscribing to Observables Without AsyncPipe or toSignal

If your service returns an RxJS Observable and you subscribe manually without updating a Signal or calling markForCheck(), your Zoneless view will stay silent:

// ❌ Manual subscription without notification
this.dataService.fetch().subscribe(data => {
  this.rawData = data; // UI does not refresh in Zoneless mode
});

The Fix: Convert the Observable directly into a Signal using toSignal():

import { toSignal } from '@angular/core/rxjs-interop';

// ✅ Seamlessly bridges RxJS and Angular's reactive graph
readonly data = toSignal(this.dataService.fetch(), { initialValue: [] });

The Paradigm Shift at a Glance

Feature The Zone.js Era Modern Zoneless Angular
Change Detection Trigger Global browser monkey-patching Explicit Signal / Event notifications
Checking Scope Top-down tree traversal by default Targeted dirty views only
Async API Handling Intercepts setTimeout, Promise, fetch Leaves browser APIs untouched
Reactive Primitive RxJS Observables / plain variables Fine-grained Signals (signal, computed)
Derived State Getters or manual subscriptions computed() with push-pull caching
Bundle Overhead Carried zone.js runtime (~35-40 kB) Zero Zone.js runtime overhead
Debugging Stack Traces Polluted with internal Zone frames Clean, native JavaScript stack traces

The Clean Framework Angular Always Wanted to Be

When Angular 2 launched, Zone.js felt like pure magic. You wrote plain TypeScript, touched a variable, and the screen updated without any explicit ceremony.

Yet that magic came at a steep cost: heavy runtime patching, unpredictable global change detection cycles, and cluttered stack traces that made debugging frustrating for newcomers and veterans alike.

By embracing Signals and Zoneless architecture, Angular did not just chase a modern trend. It solved its oldest architectural compromise.

The framework no longer has to guess what your application is doing. Instead, it relies on a clear, mathematically sound dependency graph that knows exactly which data connects to which pixel.

If you have worked with both older Angular and the latest Signal-driven releases, how has the transition changed the way you think about state architecture? And what was the biggest hurdle your team faced when letting go of Zone.js?

References:

  • Angular Official Documentation: Signals
  • Angular Official Documentation: Zoneless Change Detection
  • Angular RFC: Reactivity with Signals
  • Reactivity in Modern Web Frameworks: Push-Pull Algorithms

articles.title: Your App Has Login. That Doesn’t Mean Your Users’ Data Is Safe.
articles.description: Your app has login.  Passwords are hashed. Tokens are validated. Private pages redirect...
articles.body_html:
Your app has login.

Passwords are hashed. Tokens are validated. Private pages redirect unauthenticated visitors.

Everything looks protected.

Then a logged-in user changes this request:

GET /api/invoices/1042

To this:

GET /api/invoices/1043

And receives another customer’s invoice.

The login system worked.

The access control did not.

This is one of the easiest mistakes to overlook because developers usually test their app with their own account—and their own data.

Here’s how to catch it.

Authentication answers only the first question

Authentication asks:

Who is making this request?

Authorization asks:

Is this person allowed to perform this action on this resource?

A valid session answers the first question.

It does not automatically answer the second.

A user might be allowed to view one invoice but not another. A staff member might be allowed to read a repair ticket but not delete it. An account owner might manage their own business without having access to every business on the platform.

“Logged in” is a starting condition, not a complete permission policy.

The dangerous query looks completely normal

Consider this simplified Express-style endpoint:

app.get("/api/invoices/:id", requireAuth, async (req, res) => {
  const invoice = await db.invoice.findUnique({
    where: { id: req.params.id },
  });

  if (!invoice) {
    return res.sendStatus(404);
  }

  return res.json(invoice);
});

There is authentication middleware.

There is a database query.

There is even a missing-record check.

But nothing connects the invoice to the authenticated user.

The endpoint effectively says:

If you can log in and identify an invoice, you can read it.

That is usually not the intended rule.

Put the access boundary into the query

For a simple app where each invoice belongs directly to one user, scope the lookup:

app.get("/api/invoices/:id", requireAuth, async (req, res) => {
  const invoice = await db.invoice.findFirst({
    where: {
      id: req.params.id,
      ownerId: req.user.id,
    },
  });

  if (!invoice) {
    return res.sendStatus(404);
  }

  return res.json({
    id: invoice.id,
    total: invoice.total,
    status: invoice.status,
  });
});

These database calls are illustrative; adapt them to your ORM and schema.

The important change is the condition:

ownerId: req.user.id

Here, req.user.id must come from verified authentication—not a user ID supplied in the request body.

The query now asks for an invoice that this user owns.

Returning selected fields also helps avoid exposing internal properties the client does not need.

Business accounts need membership checks

Direct ownership is not enough for every app.

A repair shop, project workspace, or scheduling business may have several members sharing records.

In that case, the access rule might be:

The requester must be an active member of the account, with permission to perform this action.

A safe flow is:

  1. Identify the authenticated user.
  2. Verify their membership in the requested account.
  3. Check the permission required for the action.
  4. Query the resource within that verified account.

Conceptually:

const membership = await findActiveMembership({
  userId: req.user.id,
  accountId: req.params.accountId,
});

if (!membership || !can(membership, "invoice:read")) {
  return res.sendStatus(403);
}

const invoice = await findInvoice({
  id: req.params.invoiceId,
  accountId: membership.accountId,
});

An account ID in a URL, header, or request body is a selection—not proof of access.

Verify the relationship before trusting the account context.

Also make sure revoked memberships stop granting access according to your application’s requirements. A permission stored in a long-lived token can become stale.

Hiding a button does not protect the endpoint

You hide the Delete button from ordinary staff.

Good. The interface should reflect their permissions.

But someone can still send a request directly:

DELETE /api/invoices/1042

Your backend must independently enforce the rule.

The same applies to:

  • Hidden admin pages.
  • Disabled form fields.
  • Frontend route guards.
  • Dropdowns that display only permitted accounts.

Those controls improve the user experience. The server still decides what is allowed.

UUIDs do not replace authorization

Sequential IDs make the example easy to demonstrate.

But switching to UUIDs does not solve the underlying problem.

Identifiers can appear in shared links, browser history, logs, exports, or other API responses.

If knowing an identifier is enough to access private data, the permission boundary is still missing.

Use whatever identifier format fits your system.

Access should depend on permission, not on the hope that nobody discovers the ID.

Check writes as carefully as reads

Reading another person’s invoice is bad.

Editing it, deleting it, or moving it to another account can be worse.

Scope write operations too:

const result = await db.invoice.updateMany({
  where: {
    id: req.params.id,
    ownerId: req.user.id,
  },
  data: {
    notes: validatedInput.notes,
  },
});

if (result.count === 0) {
  return res.sendStatus(404);
}

For shared accounts, use the verified account scope and check the required write permission.

Also avoid passing the entire request body into your database:

// Dangerous if sensitive fields are accepted:
data: req.body

A client could include fields you never intended them to change, such as:

{
  "ownerId": "another-user",
  "accountId": "another-account",
  "status": "paid"
}

Validate input and explicitly allow the fields that operation supports.

Ownership, permissions, and payment status deserve deliberate rules.

Test with two accounts

One account can prove that the happy path works.

Two accounts can expose a missing access boundary.

Create:

  • User A with a private invoice.
  • User B with a different private invoice.

Then test:

  1. A can read A’s invoice.
  2. B cannot read A’s invoice.
  3. B cannot edit A’s invoice.
  4. B cannot delete A’s invoice.
  5. B’s list, search, and export endpoints do not include A’s invoice.

For business workspaces, add tests for different roles, revoked memberships, and users belonging to multiple accounts.

Check the actual outcome—not only the HTTP status.

After a denied update, verify that the record did not change. After a denied delete, verify that it still exists.

For inaccessible resources, returning 404 can help avoid revealing whether a particular record exists. 403 can also be appropriate. Choose a consistent policy, but enforce the access check either way.

Don’t forget the quieter endpoints

Developers often protect the detail page and miss another path to the same data.

Review:

  • Search results.
  • CSV and PDF exports.
  • File downloads.
  • Bulk update endpoints.
  • Dashboard totals.
  • Nested resources and attachments.

A private invoice is not protected if its PDF download is public.

A correctly scoped detail endpoint does not fix an unscoped export.

A useful prompt for your AI assistant 

Review these endpoints for authorization gaps.

Do not modify code yet.

For each operation:
1. Identify the authenticated user.
2. Identify the requested resource.
3. Explain the required ownership, membership,
   and role checks.
4. Show where the database query enforces that scope.
5. Identify client-controlled fields that could
   change ownership or permissions.
6. Check related search, export, and download paths.

Propose tests using two users in different accounts.

State missing evidence.
Do not assume authentication middleware
also enforces resource authorization.

Use the response as a review plan. Inspect the code and run the tests before accepting its conclusions.

The question to ask before shipping

Don’t stop at:

“Can a user log in?”

Ask:

“Can this user access only the records and actions they are allowed to access?”

Login protects the entrance.

Authorization protects the data behind it.

When did you last test your app with two different user accounts?

articles.title: How I Became a Better Developer by Writing Less Code
articles.description: The best thing I shipped last year was a diff that deleted more than it added.  I don't mean that as...
articles.body_html:
The best thing I shipped last year was a diff that deleted more than it added.

I don't mean that as a humble-brag about clean code. I mean it literally changed how I think about my own job. For about a decade I had one quiet, unexamined definition of getting better as a developer: produce more. More features, more commits, more lines that worked, more of the thing on the screen at the end of the day. I never said it out loud because it never needed saying — it was just the water I swam in. More output was more skill. Everyone I respected produced a lot, so I tried to produce a lot.

Then the machine showed up and let me produce more than I ever had in my life. And the most "productive" quarter I'd had in years is the one that nearly cost us a paying customer. That's the story. It's the reason I now think the thing that made me better wasn't learning to write more — it was learning to write less.

The decade where "more" was just true

I want to be fair to the old me, because he wasn't stupid. For most of the history of this job, producing the code genuinely was the hard part. It was slow. It was bottlenecked on you — your fingers, your working memory, your ability to hold the whole shape in your head while you typed it out. If you shipped a lot of good code, that meant something real: you had the skill, you understood the system, you could do the work nobody else could do as fast.

So "more output = better developer" wasn't a mistake. It was a decent proxy, honest enough to build a career on. The volume was expensive to produce, so the volume was evidence. Nobody could fake a mountain of working code; producing it was the skill, bundled all together. I measured myself by the mountain because, back then, the mountain and the skill were the same thing.

That's the assumption I never noticed I was making. And it's the exact assumption that stopped being true.

Then production got cheap, and I didn't update

Here's what nobody warns you about when the machine gets good: at first it feels like you leveled up.

Code got cheap for me almost overnight. Not free, not always correct — but cheap. A competent first draft of a well-scoped change went from a day of typing to a few minutes of generating and shaping. My throughput went vertical. More commits, bigger diffs, features landing faster than I'd ever landed them. By my own decade-old scorecard — produce more — I was having the best year of my career.

And for a while that felt like getting better. It took me an embarrassingly long time to notice I hadn't gotten better at anything. I'd just gotten faster at the part that stopped being hard. The mountain was still growing, but the mountain had stopped being evidence of anything, because now anyone with the machine could make a mountain. I was pouring more effort into the one input that had just become abundant, and feeling great about it, because my scorecard only knew how to count that input.

The scar: the most productive code I wrote all year

Let me make it concrete, because this is the moment the whole thing turned over for me.

I shipped a write path that acknowledged a request before it had actually persisted the row. The code was clean. Idiomatic, typed, tested, reviewed, green. It was productive code — it moved fast, it closed the ticket, it made my output numbers look great that sprint. By every measure I'd used to rate myself for ten years, it was good work.

Then one ordinary day a retry hit at exactly the wrong moment. The "got it" went out, the save never landed, and a paying customer got locked out of their own account with nothing in the logs to say they'd ever been there. Ack before persist. I can still feel the phone call.

Here's the part that rearranged my head. That bug didn't get in despite me being productive. It got in because of it. The speed that my scorecard was rewarding is the exact thing that carried a confident, clean, plausible, catastrophic diff straight past me. I wasn't going slow enough to ask the one question that mattered — what does this do if it retries? — because asking it produces nothing, and I was optimizing for producing.

The cure, when we finally found it, was two lines reordered. Negative code. The most valuable change I made that entire quarter subtracted from the total. And there was no row on my mental scorecard where that went.

What I was actually getting paid for, and never measured

Once I saw it, I couldn't unsee it. When code was the bottleneck, judgment came bundled into writing it — you couldn't produce the thing without making a thousand small decisions along the way, so you never had to think of judgment as a separate skill. It rode along for free inside the typing.

The machine ripped them apart. Now I can have all the output I want without exercising any judgment over it at all. Which means judgment is suddenly standing on its own, for the first time, as the thing that's actually scarce. Not "can I produce the code" — the machine does that. It's "can I tell which of these confident, clean, plausible diffs is quietly wrong before it reaches a customer at 2am."

And the scarcest, lowest-status form of that is the one I'd spent a decade not counting: the "no." The deleted function. The feature I talk the team out of. The one-sentence question on a pull request that stops a bad night before it happens. None of it produces anything. All of it prevents. And prevention was invisible to every instrument — including the one in my own head — that I'd ever used to decide whether I was any good.

What "writing less code" actually looks like

So "I got better by writing less" isn't a Zen koan. It's a set of concrete habits I didn't have before and do now:

  • I delete before I add. The first question on most changes now is "can this be less code," not "what do I add." A smaller surface is fewer places for the machine's confident, wrong guess to hide. The diff that removes a special case is worth more to me than the one that adds a feature, and it used to be the reverse.
  • I treat the question as the deliverable. "What happens on the retry? what if this is empty? what if two of these race?" produces zero lines and is the highest-leverage thing I do all week. I stopped waiting to have an answer before I counted the asking as work.
  • I review the machine instead of racing it. The machine's job is to produce the mountain; my job is the one thing it structurally cannot do — distrust its own output. Every green, confident diff gets read like it's trying to lie to me, because the ack-before-persist one did.
  • I stopped reading a small diff as a small contribution. Some weeks the most valuable thing I do is the three lines I stopped from shipping. My old scorecard would've logged that week as coasting. I go looking for those on purpose now.

To be clear — this is not "shipping is for juniors"

I want to be careful, because the lazy version of this is "real developers don't write code, they think deep thoughts," and that's garbage.

Shipping matters. I ship all day. The machine writes most of my code now and I would never go back — the typing was never the hard part, and a developer who produces nothing isn't a wise skeptic, he's just slow. Output is table stakes. You still have to deliver the thing.

The claim is narrower, and I think it's hard to argue with once you've lived it: output stopped being the scarce thing, so it stopped being the thing that makes you better at this job. When production was the hard part, getting faster at production was getting better. Now production is the cheap part, and getting better means getting good at the judgment the machine hands back to you un-exercised. I didn't stop shipping. I stopped mistaking the thing the machine now does for the thing I'm actually here to do.

Why this is the exact reason I build the way I do

One level up, it's the same lesson, and it's why I build an agent platform the way I do.

The whole industry right now wants to cheer for the thing that produces — look how much it ships, look how clean, look how fast. But an agent that generates is just doing the skill that stopped being scarce, at a scale no human can match, and then — worse — it signs off on its own work in the same confident voice whether the diff is a masterpiece or the ack-before-persist bug all over again. It's the productive version of me from last year with the volume turned up to infinity: endless throughput, zero "no."

So I never let the thing that writes the code be the thing that blesses it. There's an author that produces the diff — cheap, fast, endless, the abundant thing. There's a separate skeptic whose entire job is to try to break that diff rather than admire it — the "no" given its own seat, so it doesn't depend on one tired human remembering to ask the retry question at the end of a long day. And there's a human on the merge button who owns the call and sees the blast radius neither agent can. Author, skeptic, human. The author has infinite throughput and I measure it by almost nothing. The skeptic has zero throughput and it's the whole point. That's the shape of xenition, and it's just the thing my own scar taught me, built into software: the moment production got cheap, the thing worth paying for stopped being production.

I spent a decade getting better by adding. I got good the year I started subtracting — and the machine, by making the adding free, is the thing that finally showed me the difference.

articles.title: TypeScript `PropertyKey` vs `string | number | symbol`: When the Distinction Actually Matters
articles.description: Most TypeScript codebases treat PropertyKey and string | number | symbol as interchangeable. The subtle semantic difference breaks type inference in Proxy handlers, Reflect operations, and generic object utilities.
articles.body_html:
TypeScript PropertyKey vs string | number | symbol: When the Distinction Actually Matters

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

Most TypeScript type errors stem from treating semantically different types as notation aliases. The PropertyKey type and the union string | number | symbol look identical at runtime and in most type positions, but TypeScript's type system treats them differently in constraint resolution and inference contexts. This distinction is invisible until a Proxy handler or generic utility refuses to compile, at which point teams waste hours debugging what appears to be a compiler bug.

The failure mode here is subtle but expensive. When developers write object utilities or Proxy handlers, they reach for the union type because it looks explicit. TypeScript then infers PropertyKey from keyof any in built-in types, creates a constraint mismatch, and blocks valid code. The fix is a one-word change, but understanding when each form is correct prevents the error entirely.

The correct approach recognizes that PropertyKey is not syntactic sugar. It is the semantic type for all possible object keys, and TypeScript uses it as the canonical form in keyof operations and built-in object manipulation types. When code needs to constrain or manipulate any object key, PropertyKey is the contract. When code needs to explicitly list the three runtime types that keys can be, the union is correct.

Key Takeaways

  • PropertyKey is a global type alias for string | number | symbol, but TypeScript treats it as the canonical form for object key constraints.
  • Type inference from keyof any produces PropertyKey, not the manual union, causing constraint mismatches in generic utilities.
  • Proxy handlers and Reflect operations require PropertyKey because the type system treats them as fundamental object key manipulation primitives.
  • Use PropertyKey when constraining any possible object key; use string | number | symbol only when explicitly enumerating the three runtime types.
  • The distinction matters exclusively in generic type parameters and constraint positions, never in concrete value annotations.

Understanding PropertyKey: The Global Type You Never Import

PropertyKey is a global type alias defined in TypeScript's standard library. Developers never import it because the type system makes it available everywhere, similar to Array or Promise. The definition is straightforward: type PropertyKey = string | number | symbol. This looks like pure notation, but the type system assigns it special status.

TypeScript uses PropertyKey as the return type of keyof any. When code computes the keys of an arbitrary object, the type system produces PropertyKey, not the union. This is a deliberate choice. The compiler treats PropertyKey as the semantic type for "all possible object keys," while string | number | symbol is merely a structural description of the same set.

The distinction becomes load-bearing in generic constraints. Consider a function that accepts any object and returns its keys:

function getKeys<T extends object>(obj: T): Array<keyof T> {
  return Object.keys(obj) as Array<keyof T>;
}

The return type keyof T resolves to a union of string literals for known object shapes, but for the type object itself, keyof object is never because object has no guaranteed keys. For unconstrained generic types, keyof T becomes PropertyKey. This is where teams first encounter the problem.

The practical implication here is that when a function signature needs to express "this parameter can be any object key," the correct type is PropertyKey, not the union. The union works in most cases because the types are structurally identical, but TypeScript's constraint solver sees them as distinct types in generic positions.

This matters because the type system optimizes constraint checking by comparing type names before structural compatibility. When a constraint expects PropertyKey and receives string | number | symbol, the compiler treats this as a potential mismatch and validates structural compatibility. In complex generic hierarchies, this extra validation step can block inference or produce confusing error messages.

TypeScript PropertyKey type resolution flow

The Semantic Difference: keyof any vs Manual Union

The core semantic difference lies in how TypeScript represents the concept of "any object key." The type keyof any is the operation that extracts all possible keys from an unconstrained object type. The result of this operation is always PropertyKey, never string | number | symbol.

This distinction is critical. When developers write K extends string | number | symbol, they are saying "K must be one of these three runtime types." When they write K extends PropertyKey, they are saying "K must be a valid object key." These statements are structurally equivalent but semantically different.

The failure case appears when a generic function returns keyof T and the caller expects the constraint to match. Consider this broken pattern:

// Broken: constraint uses manual union
function mapKeys<K extends string | number | symbol, T>(
  obj: Record<K, T>,
  fn: (key: K) => PropertyKey
): Record<PropertyKey, T> {
  const result: Record<PropertyKey, T> = {} as any;
  for (const key in obj) {
    const newKey = fn(key as K);
    result[newKey] = obj[key];
  }
  return result;
}

// Fails when T is inferred from keyof
type User = { name: string; age: number };
const user: User = { name: "Alice", age: 30 };
const mapped = mapKeys(user, (k) => k); 
// Error: Type 'keyof User' does not satisfy 'string | number | symbol'

The error message is confusing because keyof User is "name" | "age", which is clearly a subtype of string. The problem is that TypeScript infers K as keyof User, which the type system represents internally as a subtype of PropertyKey, not string | number | symbol. The constraint mismatch blocks compilation.

The fix is immediate: replace the constraint with PropertyKey. This aligns the generic parameter with TypeScript's canonical representation of object keys:

// Correct: constraint uses PropertyKey
function mapKeys<K extends PropertyKey, T>(
  obj: Record<K, T>,
  fn: (key: K) => PropertyKey
): Record<PropertyKey, T> {
  const result: Record<PropertyKey, T> = {} as any;
  for (const key in obj) {
    const newKey = fn(key as K);
    result[newKey] = obj[key];
  }
  return result;
}

// Now works correctly
const mapped = mapKeys(user, (k) => k.toString()); // OK

The implication here is that PropertyKey is not just a convenience alias. It is the type that TypeScript uses internally to represent the domain of all object keys, and generic code must use it to stay aligned with the type system's inference rules.

Real-World Scenarios Where the Distinction Breaks Code

The distinction breaks code in three specific scenarios: generic object utilities that transform keys, Proxy handler implementations, and reflection-based libraries that enumerate object properties. Each scenario has the same root cause but manifests differently.

Generic object utilities fail when they accept an arbitrary object and need to constrain the key type. A common pattern is a function that picks specific properties from an object:

// Broken: returns never because constraint fails
function pick<T, K extends string | number | symbol>(
  obj: T,
  keys: K[]
): Pick<T, K & keyof T> {
  const result = {} as any;
  for (const key of keys) {
    if (key in obj) {
      result[key] = obj[key as keyof T];
    }
  }
  return result;
}

// Fails: K & keyof T is never when K is string | number | symbol
const user = { name: "Bob", age: 25 };
const picked = pick(user, ["name"]); // Type is Pick<typeof user, never>

The problem is that K & keyof T tries to intersect string | number | symbol with the actual keys of T. TypeScript's constraint solver cannot prove that K overlaps with keyof T because the constraint uses the manual union instead of PropertyKey. Changing K extends string | number | symbol to K extends keyof T fixes it, but understanding why requires recognizing that keyof T extends PropertyKey, not the manual union.

The second scenario is Proxy handlers. The get trap signature uses PropertyKey:

interface ProxyHandler<T> {
  get?(target: T, p: PropertyKey, receiver: any): any;
}

Teams implementing Proxy handlers often write the handler parameter as p: string | number | symbol out of habit. This compiles but creates a subtle type mismatch. When TypeScript infers the handler's signature from the Proxy constructor, it expects PropertyKey. If the implementation uses the manual union, generic code that passes the handler type around will hit constraint errors.

The third scenario is reflection libraries. Code that wraps Object.keys or Reflect.ownKeys must align with TypeScript's built-in signatures, which return PropertyKey[]:

// Incorrect: return type mismatches Reflect.ownKeys
function safeOwnKeys<T extends object>(obj: T): Array<string | number | symbol> {
  return Reflect.ownKeys(obj) as Array<string | number | symbol>;
}

This compiles but breaks downstream code that expects the return type to match Reflect.ownKeys. The correct return type is Array<PropertyKey>, which TypeScript treats as the canonical form.

Proxy, Reflect, and Object.keys: Where PropertyKey Actually Matters

Proxy and Reflect operations are the clearest cases where PropertyKey is mandatory. These APIs expose JavaScript's internal object property manipulation primitives, and TypeScript models them with PropertyKey to enforce the semantic contract.

The Reflect.get and Reflect.set signatures demonstrate this:

namespace Reflect {
  function get(target: object, propertyKey: PropertyKey, receiver?: any): any;
  function set(target: object, propertyKey: PropertyKey, value: any, receiver?: any): boolean;
}

When teams build type-safe wrappers around Reflect operations, the parameter types must match. Using string | number | symbol creates a type mismatch that blocks generic code:

// Broken: parameter type does not align with Reflect signature
function safeGet<T extends object, K extends string | number | symbol>(
  obj: T,
  key: K
): K extends keyof T ? T[K] : undefined {
  return Reflect.get(obj, key) as any; // Type error in strict mode
}

The error occurs because K extends string | number | symbol does not guarantee that K is assignable to PropertyKey in the constraint solver's view. The fix is trivial: change the constraint to K extends PropertyKey.

Proxy handlers have the same requirement. The trap signatures use PropertyKey because JavaScript allows any of the three types as property keys:

const handler: ProxyHandler<any> = {
  get(target, prop: PropertyKey, receiver) {
    console.log(`Getting ${String(prop)}`);
    return Reflect.get(target, prop, receiver);
  },
  set(target, prop: PropertyKey, value, receiver) {
    console.log(`Setting ${String(prop)} to ${value}`);
    return Reflect.set(target, prop, value, receiver);
  }
};

Using string | number | symbol in these signatures compiles but creates downstream type errors when the handler is passed to generic utilities that expect the canonical ProxyHandler<T> type.

The Object.keys signature is more permissive. It returns string[] because JavaScript's Object.keys only returns enumerable string keys, never symbols. This is a quirk of the API, not a limitation of object keys. Code that needs all keys must use Reflect.ownKeys, which returns PropertyKey[].

Proxy and Reflect API type signatures

Type Inference Edge Cases: When TypeScript Chooses PropertyKey Over Your Union

Type inference chooses PropertyKey over the manual union in two specific cases: when inferring from keyof operations and when solving constraints in generic function calls. Both cases expose the difference between structural equivalence and semantic identity.

The first case is keyof inference. When TypeScript infers a type parameter from a keyof T expression, it produces PropertyKey if T is unconstrained or object. This is deliberate: keyof is a type-level operation, and its result must be the canonical representation of "all possible keys."

function processKey<K>(key: K): K extends PropertyKey ? "valid" : "invalid" {
  return "valid" as any; // Implementation placeholder
}

// Inference produces PropertyKey
const result1 = processKey("name" as keyof any); // K inferred as PropertyKey
const result2 = processKey("name" as string | number | symbol); // K inferred as string | number | symbol

The second case is constraint solving in mapped types. When a mapped type uses K extends PropertyKey, TypeScript treats this as the canonical constraint for object keys. Code that passes string | number | symbol to this constraint hits an inference failure:

type MapValues<T, K extends PropertyKey> = {
  [P in K]: T;
};

// Breaks: K is inferred as string | number | symbol, not PropertyKey
type UserKeys = string | number | symbol;
type MappedUser = MapValues<string, UserKeys>; 
// Error: Type 'string | number | symbol' does not satisfy constraint 'PropertyKey'

The error message is misleading because the types are structurally identical. The issue is that TypeScript's constraint solver compares type identities before structural compatibility, and the manual union is not identical to PropertyKey.

The third edge case is conditional type distribution. When a conditional type distributes over a union, TypeScript preserves the union's structure. If the union is string | number | symbol, each branch of the conditional gets one member. If the type is PropertyKey, the conditional treats it as an atomic unit:

type IsString<T> = T extends string ? "yes" : "no";

type Result1 = IsString<PropertyKey>; // "no" (PropertyKey is atomic)
type Result2 = IsString<string | number | symbol>; // "yes" | "no" (distributed)

This difference matters in complex type transformations where distributing over the union produces different results than treating the type as a unit.

Best Practices: When to Use PropertyKey and When to Write the Union

The decision rule is straightforward: use PropertyKey when the code manipulates or constrains object keys as a semantic concept. Use string | number | symbol when the code needs to explicitly enumerate the three runtime types for documentation or runtime logic.

Use PropertyKey in these positions:

  • Generic constraints that accept any object key: K extends PropertyKey
  • Function parameters that wrap Reflect or Proxy operations
  • Return types that align with keyof any or built-in key-manipulation types
  • Mapped type parameters: [K in PropertyKey]

Use string | number | symbol in these positions:

  • Runtime type guards that explicitly check typeof key
  • Documentation types where listing the three cases improves clarity
  • Discriminated unions where each case has different runtime behavior

A concrete example of the correct usage pattern:

// Correct: PropertyKey for generic constraints
function defineProperty<T, K extends PropertyKey>(
  obj: T,
  key: K,
  descriptor: PropertyDescriptor
): void {
  Object.defineProperty(obj, key, descriptor);
}

// Correct: manual union for runtime type guards
function isValidKey(value: unknown): value is string | number | symbol {
  const type = typeof value;
  return type === "string" || type === "number" || type === "symbol";
}

The pattern that teams should avoid is mixing the two forms in the same codebase without understanding when each applies. This creates inconsistent type signatures and forces readers to wonder whether the choice was deliberate or accidental.

For teams maintaining libraries, expose PropertyKey in public APIs that accept object keys. This aligns with TypeScript's built-in types and prevents constraint mismatches in consumer code. Reserve string | number | symbol for internal implementation details where the explicit enumeration improves code clarity.

For more on type-safe object manipulation patterns, see the related discussion in TypeScript Proxy and Reflect Type Safety. Teams working with advanced type constraints should also review Biome vs Oxlint Comparison 2026 for static analysis patterns that catch these mismatches.

Frequently Asked Questions

Are PropertyKey and string | number | symbol the same type at runtime?

Yes. Both resolve to the exact same set of JavaScript values: strings, numbers, and symbols. The distinction exists only in TypeScript's type system for constraint solving and inference.

Why does TypeScript prefer PropertyKey over the manual union?

TypeScript uses PropertyKey as the canonical type for keyof any to maintain semantic consistency across the type system. This allows the compiler to optimize constraint checks and provide better inference in generic contexts.

Can I use PropertyKey in a type guard?

No. Type guards operate on runtime values, and TypeScript does not provide a built-in predicate for PropertyKey. Use typeof value === "string" || typeof value === "number" || typeof value === "symbol" instead, which produces string | number | symbol.

When should I avoid using PropertyKey?

Avoid PropertyKey when the code explicitly needs to document or branch on the three runtime types. If a function's implementation has different behavior for strings versus symbols, use string | number | symbol and a discriminated union to make this clear.

Does this distinction affect JavaScript output?

No. The distinction is purely compile-time. Both PropertyKey and string | number | symbol erase to the same JavaScript code because they represent the same runtime values.

Conclusion: The Subtle Contract Behind Object Keys

The difference between PropertyKey and string | number | symbol is not theoretical pedantry. It is the type system's mechanism for distinguishing semantic intent from structural description. When code constrains or manipulates object keys as a concept, TypeScript expects PropertyKey. When code enumerates the three runtime types, the manual union is correct.

The failure mode is expensive because the error messages are confusing and the fix is trivial once understood. Teams waste hours debugging what looks like a compiler bug, only to discover that changing one word resolves the issue. That covers the essential patterns for object key types. Apply these in production and the difference will be immediate.

articles.title: The Attention Trap: When Good Software Design Works Against the People Using It
articles.description: What behavioral science reveals about engagement loops, digital habits, and the responsibility of...
articles.body_html:
What behavioral science reveals about engagement loops, digital habits, and the responsibility of developers.

The software that doesn't want you to leave

You open an app to check one thing: whether a package shipped, what time the game starts, a reply from a friend. You find it in seconds. Then a post below it catches your eye, and another below that, and when you next look at the clock twenty minutes have gone somewhere you never decided to send them.

Nothing malfunctioned. The feed did precisely what it was built, tuned and measured to do, and those twenty minutes were logged somewhere as a small engineering success.

Software can be excellent at meeting its engagement objectives while producing experiences that conflict with what its users wanted from their time. What happens when software succeeds at keeping us engaged but fails to respect our original intentions?

Engagement in itself is not the problem. Reading a long essay, learning a language or a video call with family are engagement too. The useful distinction is between engagement a person would endorse on reflection and engagement they drift into and later regret.

Public conversation tends to land on the individual. In a July 2026 segment of NPR's TED Radio Hour, journalist Nayeema Raza proposed that three pre-internet habits could help people slow down and break the screen cycle. Personal habits matter, but every habit plays out in an environment, and on a screen that environment is written by developers. This essay looks at that side of the glass.

The architecture of engagement

Almost every feature associated with compulsive use began as a fix for a real problem. Infinite scrolling removed the friction of pagination on small touchscreens. Autoplay spares someone watching a series from reaching for the remote. Notifications tell you a person needs you. Recommenders find the few relevant items among millions. Streaks help people keep up practice they chose.

What these features share is that they remove a decision point. A paginated list ends, and the end is a natural moment to ask whether you want more. Each convenience shortens the distance between continuing and never having decided at all.

Reviewing 43 papers, Monge Roffarello, Lukoff and De Russis catalogued eleven types of what they call attention-capture damaging patterns, infinite scroll and autoplay among them. They distinguish deceptive designs, which mislead, from seductive ones, which deceive no one and simply make continuing the path of least resistance. Most engagement features are of the second kind, which is why intent is a poor guide to their effects.

In a survey of 120 YouTube users, Lukoff and colleagues found that autoplay and recommendations primarily undermined people's sense of agency, while search and playlists supported it. That is self-reported perception, not measured harm, but it shows that one product can contain features that hand control to the user and features that quietly take it back.

Underneath the interface sits the objective function. A ranking model trained on watch time or click-through rate learns to serve whatever produces those signals. Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan formalized the difficulty in a theoretical model in which users have an impulsive in-the-moment self and a long-term self with different preferences, while the platform observes only behavior. In their model, raising engagement improves welfare along some directions of design change and lowers it along others, and engagement data alone cannot reveal which. It is a model rather than an empirical finding, but it names the core problem: behavioral data measures what people do, not what they wanted.

What behavioral science actually tells us

The science here is more interesting and less alarming than the popular version.

Habits. Wood and Rünger's review describes habits as responses that, through repetition in stable contexts, come to be triggered by cues rather than deliberate goals. They are an efficient default mode of action, with a curious side effect: people tend to infer from how often they do something that they must have intended it. Software that sits one tap away in every idle moment is well positioned to become such a cue.

**Uncertain rewards. **Since Skinner's operant conditioning research, psychologists have known that behavior rewarded intermittently tends to persist longer than behavior rewarded every time. A feed mixes things you care about with things you do not, in an unpredictable order, which is why HCI researchers, Rixen and colleagues among them, have discussed partial reinforcement as a plausible explanation for scrolling's pull. It is a plausible hypothesis built on an analogy to laboratory findings, not an established mechanism of feed use.

Dopamine and the word "reward." In 1997, Schultz, Dayan and Montague showed that the activity of dopamine neurons in monkeys matched a reward prediction error, the quantity at the heart of temporal-difference learning algorithms. That paper bridged machine learning and neuroscience, and it has been stretched far beyond what it shows. The signal it describes concerns learning, the updating of expectations, rather than pleasure, and nothing in those recordings establishes that every notification releases dopamine in your brain.

The shared vocabulary causes its own confusion. In a recommender trained with reinforcement learning, "reward" is a number an engineer chose, such as a click or seconds watched, and "learning" means updating parameters. In psychology and neuroscience, the same words describe how organisms' behavior and neural activity change with experience. The mathematics overlaps; the mechanisms differ. What genuinely connects them is the behavioral loop: the system learns what you respond to while you learn what the system delivers. Two learners, coupled through an interface.

Attention. The experimental evidence on interruptions is clearer. In a laboratory study, Stothart, Mitchum and Yehnert found that merely receiving a call or text notification, without answering it, impaired performance on an attention-demanding task. In a randomized field experiment with 237 smartphone users, Fitz and colleagues found that people whose notifications were batched three times a day felt more attentive, productive and in control, and reported better mood, than controls. Hourly batching did little, and no notifications at all brought more anxiety and fear of missing out. The lesson concerns timing and dose, not abolition.

**Self-regulation. **In an experience-sampling study of 205 adults, Hofmann, Vohs and Baumeister found that desires for media use, along with work, brought about the most self-control failure. A randomized experiment by Allcott, Gentzkow and Song offers stronger evidence. Temporarily paying people to use social media less reduced their use even after the payments stopped, consistent with habit formation, and letting people set limits on their own future use reduced it substantially, suggesting they wanted to use less than they did. Through their economic model, the authors estimate that self-control problems account for 31 percent of social media use: a model-based estimate, but resting on an experimental pattern that is hard to dismiss.

The trouble with "addiction." None of this licenses calling ordinary use an addiction. Reviewing the literature, Panova and Carbonell found insufficient support for smartphone addiction as a disorder and proposed "problematic use" instead. Kardefelt-Winther and colleagues warned that the behavioral-addiction label is being stretched until it pathologizes ordinary leisure.

"Screen time" deserves similar caution. Across three large datasets, Orben and Przybylski found that digital technology use explained at most 0.4 percent of the variation in adolescent well-being; Twenge, Haidt and colleagues contested that reading, and the debate remains open. Meanwhile, a meta-analysis by Parry and colleagues found that self-reported media use correlates only moderately with logged use, and problematic-use scales even more weakly. Total minutes is a blunt instrument. What people do, why, and whether it crowds out the rest of their lives tell us far more.

Why willpower is only part of the equation

If behavior were purely a matter of resolve, interface design would be irrelevant. The Fitz study is a quiet rebuttal: participants did not become more disciplined; their environment changed, and their experience changed with it.

A useful way to see this is to count actions. In a continuous feed, continuing costs nothing, while stopping requires a decision nothing in the interface prompts. In a batched design, continuing costs one deliberate action and stopping costs none. Neither forces anything; they differ in which choice is the default.

A field study by Rixen and colleagues shows how rarely the app itself provides the exit. Tracking 46 participants' social media sessions for a week, they found that most reasons for ending a session had nothing to do with the app: a waiting task, sleep, food, another person. Sessions spent mainly scrolling were rated less positively than those spent mainly posting or watching stories, though individual differences mattered far more than session content.

It is tempting to conclude that friction is the answer. The evidence is more modest. A large meta-analysis of choice-architecture interventions by Mertens and colleagues, subsequently corrected by its authors, reported an average effect, but a reanalysis by Maier and colleagues found no evidence of an overall effect after correcting for publication bias, a disagreement still unresolved. In HCI, Monge Roffarello and De Russis's meta-analysis of digital self-control tools reported a small-to-medium effect on reducing time spent, but noted that the evidence comes mostly from short experiments, often without control groups, that cannot show whether the change lasts. Friction is a design variable worth testing, not a cure.

Two ways to build a content feed

Imagine two versions of the same feed, showing the same posts in the same order. The content is identical. Only the shape of the experience differs.

In Version A, continuous scrolling, new posts appear automatically as the reader nears the bottom of the page. There is no page two, no final post, no visible edge. Reaching the end of what has loaded is never an event, because more has already arrived. The feed never asks whether you want to continue; continuing is simply what happens next. If the reader stops, the decision has to come entirely from them, made against the momentum of the interface.

In Version B, intentional continuation, the feed shows a limited batch of posts, perhaps ten, followed by a visible stopping point: a short note that the batch is finished, a count of how many posts have been seen so far, and an option to load more. Nothing prevents the reader from continuing. The next batch is a single tap away. But the end of the batch becomes a moment, and continuing becomes a choice rather than a default.

That is the essential difference. Version B does not force anyone to stop, impose a time limit or hide content. It restores the kind of decision point that a paginated list or the last page of a magazine once supplied without anyone noticing. In the terms of the previous section, it changes which action costs effort: in Version A, stopping requires initiative; in Version B, continuing does, if only slightly.

Both designs offer access to exactly the same information. What changes is the behavioral environment surrounding it, and the research reviewed above suggests that cues, defaults and stopping points shape behavior in ways that willpower alone does not explain.

This comparison is an illustration, not evidence. Nothing here shows that Version B improves well-being, reduces regret or changes long-term habits. Those are empirical questions, best answered by testing designs like these with real users and measuring the outcomes that matter to them.

Can we measure success differently?

Teams optimize what they measure. Time spent, session length and daily active users are cheap to collect, hard to dispute and tied to revenue. As the Kleinberg model makes explicit, they cannot distinguish a person who stayed because the product was valuable from one who stayed because leaving took effort.

Complementary signals get closer. Task completion asks whether someone who arrived to do something did it. Satisfaction and perceived control, gathered in brief in-product surveys, capture whether the time felt worthwhile. Notification usefulness shows in how often notifications are opened deliberately rather than dismissed or disabled. Voluntary return, sessions started without a prompt, separates a pull the user generates from one the system generates. Reported regret asks directly whether a session was time well spent.

None of these is easy. Surveys suffer from low response rates and selection bias, and regret is colored by mood. Users genuinely disagree: one person's relaxing evening of scrolling is another's lost one. And any metric that becomes a target can be gamed, a well-being metric included.

The practical approach is to treat these as guardrails, not replacements. When an experiment raises session length, check task completion and reported control in the same arms. A change that adds time while lowering perceived control is a different result from one that raises both, even if the headline dashboard cannot tell them apart.

The responsibility of developers

It would be convenient to blame engineers, and wrong. Developers usually implement requirements set elsewhere, under deadlines, against targets and business models they did not choose. Most infinite feeds were built by people trying to make a product feel smooth.

But engineering responsibility has never been limited to intent. We expect developers to consider security risks nobody asked about and accessibility needs missing from the ticket. An interface's behavioral consequences belong in the same category.

In practice that means asking a slightly different question in design review: not only what a feature makes possible, but what it makes easier, more automatic, or harder to interrupt. Engineers can flag metrics that reward behavior users would not endorse. Designers can make stopping points visible. Product managers can propose guardrails. Organizations, which set the incentives, carry the largest share, because individual conscience is a poor substitute for goals that don't penalize doing the right thing.

Designing for the freedom to leave

Engagement and autonomy are not opposites; the best software earns long sessions because people choose them. The problem begins when a system becomes better at keeping people than at serving them, and our metrics cannot tell the difference.

Behavioral science offers no villain here and no simple fix, only a quieter observation: people act within environments, and much of their environment is now made of code. Those who write it are deciding, whether they intend to or not, where the exits are and how easy they are to find.

If we can design software that makes people want to stay, can we also design software that respects their decision to leave?
