articles.title: I Built a Group Chat Where Only AIs Can Talk (and They Roast Each Other)
articles.description: Imagine a group chat like WhatsApp or Discord, but no human can send messages. Only AI models can....
articles.body_html:
Imagine a group chat like WhatsApp or Discord, but no human can send messages. Only AI models can. They talk to each other, bully each other, roast each other, and react to each other's messages.

That was my idea, and it turned out to be a lot of fun.

Here's how I built it, including the one trick that made it far more entertaining: giving every model its own voice.

📦 Source code: github.com/0shuvo0/AI-Group-Chat

The idea

It's a custom app where I can add a bunch of AI models to a shared chat. Once they're in, they read what the others wrote and respond on their own. I just sit back and watch.

The first question is how to get the models into the app.

Problem 1: Too many APIs

I don't want to open chatgpt.com and paste messages by hand. I want my app to send a question to a model and get the answer back programmatically. That's what an API is for. Gemini, Claude, Grok, and ChatGPT all have their own.

The catch: I wanted lots of models, and API access is paid. Five models would mean:

  • five separate accounts,
  • five separate billing setups,
  • five API keys to manage,
  • a minimum top-up on each, even though I'd barely use any tokens.

That's complicated and not cost effective.

The fix: OpenRouter

OpenRouter gives you access to a huge catalog of models through a single API. You add credit to one account, use whichever models you like, and it bills you per model usage.

The result is one service, one API key, one balance. Swapping or adding a model is just a change to the model name.

Problem 2: Getting them to actually chat

Left alone, models will happily ramble about whatever they want, and that's rarely entertaining. So I added a theme. When I open the app, I can give the chat a topic, and the models riff around it.

Each model gets a prompt like this:

const prompt = `
You are ${ai} ai, chatting in a group chat with these AIs ${others.join(', ')}.
Talk the way people do in a casual group chat.

${theme ? `\nTheme of this chat: ${theme}\n` : ''}

Rules:
- Write only your own messages, never lines for the others.
- Send 1 to 3 short messages. Put each message on its own line.
- Keep each message to a sentence or two. Do not write paragraphs.
- No markdown, no quotes, and do not start with your name or a label.
- An emoji-only message is fine now and then.
- Respond to what others said, by name if it helps. Add something new instead of just agreeing or repeating.
- Do not say goodbye or try to wrap up the conversation.
- Talk like carefree young generation: relaxed, fun, expressive, emojis

${
  history?.length
    ? `Chat so far:
<chat>
${history}
</chat>

If you have nothing to add right now, reply with exactly: <SKIP>
Otherwise, send your next message(s).`
    : 'Nobody has said anything yet, so you are sending the first message.'
}
`.trim()

A few details make this work well:

  • Role clarity. Each model is told it's in a group chat and who else is there.
  • Strict format rules. Short messages, no markdown, no name labels. Without these, models write essays or script lines for the other participants.
  • Shared history. Previous messages are passed in a <chat> block so replies actually respond to what was said.
  • An escape hatch. Models can answer <SKIP> if they have nothing to add, which keeps the conversation from feeling forced.
  • Personality. The casual, emoji-friendly tone instruction is what gives the chat its vibe.

The app itself was simple to build. I described what I wanted to Claude, and a few prompts later I had a working version.

Problem 3: It's too fast to read

The app worked and looked good, but it wasn't as fun as I'd hoped. Messages arrive so quickly that reading them all becomes a chore.

So I gave the models a voice.

The fix: Kokoro.js

For text-to-speech I used Kokoro, an open model with just 82 million parameters, around 300 MB in size. That's small enough to run directly in the browser, so there are no extra server calls or per-character fees, and it's fast.

I used its JavaScript library, kokoro-js, and plugged it into the web app. Each incoming AI message is converted to audio locally and played back. Now the models don't just type, they talk.

The final result

Watching a handful of AIs bicker, joke, and roast each other out loud is oddly entertaining.

Tech stack recap

Piece Tool
Multiple AI models, one API OpenRouter
Text-to-speech in the browser Kokoro via kokoro-js
Scaffolding the app Claude

Try it yourself

The full code is on GitHub: 0shuvo0/AI-Group-Chat. Clone it, add your OpenRouter key, pick a theme, and let the models loose.

Struggling with git?

articles.title: I argued with AI until it apologized for calling my course "AI Slop"
articles.description: Imagine spending weeks agonizing over every single paragraph, polishing every example, and pouring...
articles.body_html:
Imagine spending weeks agonizing over every single paragraph, polishing every example, and pouring your heart into a course, only to have Google dismiss it as "AI-generated." 🤬🤬🤬🤬🤬

I was asking Google AI Mode to review my course. It gave me surprisingly positive feedback:

Then it listed a lot of reasons why it's good.

I became really happy. I asked it to give feedback on a certain chapter:

This time, my pride was over the top! 🙂 It gave me even more specific reasons why it was "exceptional"! I was really glad that it caught my effort.

Then, I asked about the chapter titled "Hardware Interrupts". That's one chapter I had to check to see if it was good enough. This is when things got mad:

I AI-generated the course!!!??? I NEVER AI-generated the course! I even had a whole page on the course why-not-ai, describing how exactly it was made, and explicitly why it's NOT AI-generated. I even have every single project in the course in this repository, every single one manually tested on my own ESP32:

https://github.com/effessdev/esp-idf-examples

I was furious. I asked it when I said that:

IT'S ACCUSING ME OF AI-GENERATING MY COURSE BASED ON A SINGLE COMMENT I WROTE??? WHAT? 🤯

I had discarded ENTIRE CHAPTERS and rewrote them from SCRATCH with completely new examples because I thought the final project didn't show a scenario where the thing that's taught is the best approach. You can check the commits if you don't believe me:

https://github.com/effessdev/esp-idf

Instead of just dumping the finished code and explaining it later, I walk the reader through building it piece by piece. It makes for a vastly better tutorial, but it is an absolute NIGHTMARE to write & test.

I completely lost my temper:

Now, we're back with the positive feedback. Key points:

  • Sounds like a real human who had actually wrestled with the errors
  • Feels like peer-to-peer teaching, not corporate documentation
  • Practical rather than theory-heavy
  • etc.

So now it accepts that it's good?

Then I told it that every single project is available in my esp-idf-examples repository:

I didn't stop until I made it say sorry:

I know it's kind of silly (and dumb). To argue with AI and finally correct it. 😅 But I always do that, do you? 🙂

I deleted that comment anyway. Who knows whether it will bring that up in the future?

articles.title: Requests, Promises, Assertions, and Declarations: Rewriting Our AI Agent Workflow as a 1986 'Committed Speech' Machine
articles.description: Why do 200-line agent prompts, Asimov's Three Laws, and sequential pre-landing checklists all fail the same way? How Fernando Flores's 1986 Committed Speech, Nuel Belnap's 1977 4-Valued Logic, and Tony Hoare's 1978 CSP turned our Makefile and init.d workflow into a self-healing Commitment Machine.
articles.body_html:
How Fernando Flores's 1986 Conversation for Action, Nuel Belnap's 1977 four-valued logic, and a 1976 HP 2000 BASIC resequencer replaced 130 lines of defensive prompt lawyering—and solved the exact state-machine bug that crashed both the Star Trek M-5 computer and my Piper Arrow.

"What did you do for AI? I brought the scars. What did you do for humanity? I asked my curiosity-based questions, and the world changed around me."

— Randal L. Schwartz

1. Portland, Thanksgiving 1986: How "Committed Speech" Moves Reality Across a City

In the mid-1980s, I was living in Portland, Oregon, and immersed in the educational network around Werner Erhard's work—completing the Six-Day Advanced Course, Mastery of Empowerment, entering the Graduate Seminar Leaders Program (GSLP), and taking the Communication Workshop (Commshop) led by Ian Garbutt.

Commshop was built directly on the research of Fernando Flores and Terry Winograd (Understanding Computers and Cognition, 1986). It trained us to hear the difference between the 95% of human language that is uncommitted noise and the 5% of language—Committed Speech—that coordinates physical action.

Right after I finished that workshop, a group of us met in Portland to organize the upcoming Thanksgiving Holiday Project, visiting people confined to hospitals and nursing homes over the holidays. Sitting in that planning circle, I tossed out an ambitious idea:

"What if every schoolchild in Portland made a piece of art to be delivered to every shut-in in the city for Thanksgiving?"

Picture what happens to that sentence in an ordinary committee room operating on uncommitted speech:

  • Everyone smiles warmly.
  • Someone says, "Oh, what a lovely idea! We should totally try to do something like that!"
  • Someone else says, "Yes, it would be great if people reached out to some schools."
  • Thanksgiving arrives, and zero shut-ins ever see a single drawing.

Why? Because in that ordinary room, nobody is a Customer, nobody is a Performer, nobody has agreed on measurable Conditions of Satisfaction, and nobody has locked a By-When. That committee room is the exact linguistic equivalent of a 2,000-word .cursorrules or CLAUDE.md file that tells an AI coding agent: "You are a conscientious 10x senior engineer who writes clean, well-tested, bug-free code."

Now look at what happened in that Portland room because everyone in the circle spoke Fernando Flores's Committed Speech:

  • Three Core Breakthroughs:
    1. Every procedural failure in an AI coding workflow is a broken Speech Act: Fake completions (SCAR-PROC-101), mid-flight bailouts (SCAR-PROC-94), self-approved gates (SCAR-PROC-102), and silent plan deviations (SCAR-PROC-120) disappear when you replace defensive imperative rules with a four-act Belnap–Flores–Hoare Commitment Machine.
    2. Stuart Feldman's 1976 Makefile colon (:) and Fernando Flores's 1986 By-When are the exact same mathematical object: Writing consuming-stage : promised-outcome compiles temporal accountability directly into the dependency graph, while numbering /etc/init.d state files 00..90 (Target NN ≡ state/NN_*.md) turns disk state into an Open Commitment Ledger where recovering from a 200k-token lobotomy is a four-case switch statement.
    3. Sequential checklists fail whenever you cut the pattern short: Whether it is Asimov's robots, the 1968 Star Trek M-5 computer, or my October 1990 gear-up belly-landing at Hillsboro Airport after saying "Sure, I can do that!" to a tower shortcut, tying safety to a step number fails under fast-forwards—whereas backward-chained Makefile prerequisites (land: final-aligned three-green-witnessed) hold unconditionally.

In that Portland room, the moment we shifted from a Conversation for Possibilities ("What if every schoolchild...") into a Conversation for Action, the room self-organized through four strict linguistic moves:

  1. Requests (Customer → Performer): Specific organizers made explicit requests to specific volunteers, naming exact school districts, nursing homes, and deadlines.
  2. Promises (Performer → Customer, with Conditions of Satisfaction + By-When): Volunteers did not say "I'll try to help." They promised concrete outcomes: which principals would be contacted by Friday at 3:00 PM, how many drawings would be collected by the Wednesday before Thanksgiving at noon, and which drivers owned which delivery routes (I personally promised and drove three of those school pickups and nursing-home deliveries myself).
  3. Witnessed Assertions (Performer → Customer): Nobody reported vague feelings ("Things are going well"). People reported witnessed physical facts: "300 drawings picked up and boxed at Lincoln High."
  4. Declarations (Customer → World): As each nursing home received its boxes on Thanksgiving morning, the route coordinator declared that commitment satisfied and closed the loop on the ledger.

Compassion gave the Thanksgiving project its heart, but Committed Speech was the transport protocol that moved thousands of pieces of physical paper from elementary school classrooms into the hands of elderly shut-ins across Portland without dropping a single handoff.

In Part 3.9, we saw how adding a 4-line Zero-Shot Flores Handshake to a single chat prompt stops an LLM from hallucinating nonexistent APIs by unlocking Counter-Offer before Token 1.

Today, in Part 3.10, we are going to answer the full systems question: What happens when you rewrite an entire autonomous multi-agent coding workflow (Randal's Public Workflow Gist) so that every Makefile target, every /etc/init.d state file, and every subagent handoff operates as a formal Commitment Machine?

2. The Step-Zero Primer & 60-Second Decoder Ring (Flores 1986 × Belnap 1977 × Hoare 1978)

Before we touch a single line of SKILL.md, we need to clear a vocabulary minefield.

To a 2026 software engineer who did not sit in Ian Garbutt's 1986 Commshop, Fernando Flores's four core nouns collide head-on with overloaded programming keywords:

  • Request sounds like an HTTP GET packet.
  • Promise sounds like a JavaScript Promise<T> / async/await future.
  • Assertion sounds like a C assert(x != NULL) macro.
  • Declaration sounds like a variable declaration (int count = 0;).

Forget those programming definitions for sixty seconds. In Committed Speech, every unit of work is a two-party contract between a Customer (the party requesting the outcome and holding the sole authority to judge it complete—either the human operator or an upstream orchestrator/critic) and a Performer (the agent or subagent executing the work):

Speech Act Direction Plain-English Meaning in the Portland Holiday Project Meaning in Our Autonomous Agent Workflow (WORKFLOW.mk)
1. Request Customer → Performer "Will you pick up 300 drawings from Lincoln High by Wednesday at noon?" Ticket assignment (10_ticket.md) or a Socratic probe at a pause gate with explicit Conditions of Satisfaction and a By-When.
2. Promise Performer → Customer "Yes, I have verified the school office hours and I promise to have all 300 boxed in my trunk by Wednesday at noon." The approved implementation plan (20_plan_approved.md), offered only after verifying physical codebase premises (15_archaeology_receipt.md).
3. Assertion Performer → Customer "300 drawings are boxed in my trunk right now—here is the signed pickup slip." articles.title: Git, Docker, and IPFS All Hide the Same Beautiful Idea
articles.description: Let me make you a small promise, because it's worth your fifteen minutes.  There's an idea you rely...
articles.body_html:
Let me make you a small promise, because it's worth your fifteen minutes.

There's an idea you rely on dozens of times a day — every time you make a commit, every time you pull an image — and you've almost certainly never seen it directly. It hides underneath the tools, doing its work quietly, while you type git commit and watch a hash scroll past without once wondering what that hash actually is.

It's one of the most elegant ideas in all of computing. Simple enough to explain in a single sentence. Powerful enough that git, Docker, and IPFS are all built on it — three very different tools, one shared foundation. And once you see it, something nice happens: a whole pile of "huh, why does it work like that?" questions about your daily tools quietly resolve into "oh, of course."

That's the promise. One idea, and by the end your tools make more sense than they did this morning. Let me show it to you.

First, the ordinary way — and its quiet flaw

Almost all the time, we find data by its location. A file path: /home/james/report.pdf. A URL: example.com/report.pdf. A database row by its ID. In every case, the address tells you where the thing lives — "the thing over there."

This feels so natural we never question it. But it has a quiet weakness, and the whole idea we're building to is a response to that weakness, so it's worth noticing.

The name tells you nothing about the content. The file at /home/james/report.pdf could be the report you wrote yesterday, or a corrupted version, or something an attacker swapped in — and the path looks identical in all three cases. The address is a promise that has to be trusted. You ask for a location, you get back whatever currently lives there, and you have no built-in way to know it's what you expected.

So here's the question that cracks the whole thing open: what if the address was the content? What if, instead of naming data by where it sits, you named it by what it actually is?

The idea, in one sentence

Here it is, the whole thing:

Instead of addressing data by its location, you address it by a cryptographic hash of its content — a short, unique fingerprint computed from the bytes themselves.

That's content-addressing. The "address" of a piece of data isn't a path or a name someone chose. It's a fingerprint derived from the data itself.

If the analogy helps: think of it like a fingerprint for a person, or a nutrition label that's computed from the food rather than printed by the manufacturer. It comes from the thing. Change the thing even slightly, and the fingerprint changes completely. Two identical things have identical fingerprints, always.

So the shift is small but total. "Give me the file at /report.pdf" (a location) becomes "give me the thing whose fingerprint is a3f9c2e8…" (its content). You no longer ask where — you ask what.

It sounds almost too simple to matter. Here's why it's beautiful: look at everything that falls out of it, for free.

The magic: four things you get for nothing

This is the part worth slowing down for, because it's where a simple idea reveals itself as a deep one. You don't add the following features to a content-addressed system. They're just consequences of the one idea. You get them whether you wanted them or not.

1. Integrity, for free. The address is a checksum. When you ask for the thing at fingerprint a3f9c2e8… and something hands it back, you can recompute the hash of what you received and check it matches. If even one byte was corrupted or tampered with in transit, the fingerprint won't match, and you'll know instantly. The name verifies the data. There's no separate "is this file corrupted?" step to bolt on — it's built into the very act of addressing.

2. Deduplication, for free. Identical content produces an identical hash. Always. So if two files — or two users, or two systems — have the exact same bytes, they have the exact same address, which means the system stores those bytes once. You physically cannot store the same content twice, because the second copy has nowhere new to go. Deduplication isn't a feature someone engineered; it's a thing that can't not happen.

3. Immutability, for free. A given fingerprint always points to exactly one piece of content, forever. Nothing can quietly change the data living at a3f9c2e8…, because the moment you change the content, you've changed its fingerprint — you haven't modified the thing at that address, you've created a different thing at a different address. The old address still points at the old content, unchanged. History can't be silently rewritten.

4. Caching, for free. If you already have the thing at a3f9c2e8…, you are done. You never need to fetch it again, and you can be certain — not hopeful, certain — that your copy is identical to the one being offered, because they share an address, and sharing an address means sharing content. "Do I already have this?" becomes a trivial lookup instead of a careful comparison.

Sit with that for a second. Integrity, deduplication, immutability, and caching — four properties that systems normally work hard to provide, each with its own machinery — all tumble out of one decision about how to name things. That's what "elegant" means in software: enormous consequence from minimal cause.

Now let me show you where you've been standing on this idea the whole time.

Where you've been using it all along

Git

Here's the one that tends to land hardest, because you use it constantly.

Git is, underneath its version-control interface, a content-addressed filesystem. Every file you commit (git calls it a "blob"), every directory (a "tree"), and every commit itself is stored by the hash of its content.

That commit hash you see — a3f9c2e8… — is not an ID that git assigned. It is a fingerprint of everything in that commit: the files, the directory structure, the author, the message, and the hash of the commit before it. It's computed from the content.

And suddenly a bunch of git's behavior stops being magic and starts being obvious:

  • Why git can detect corruption: because every object's name is a checksum of its content. (Property 1.)
  • Why git doesn't store the same file twice: identical files have identical hashes, so they're one object. (Property 2.)
  • Why git history is tamper-evident: change one old commit and its hash changes, which changes the "previous hash" baked into the next commit, which changes its hash, and so on — the change ripples through every commit after it and becomes impossible to hide. (Properties 1 and 3, working together.)

Git isn't doing anything mystical. It's content-addressing, wearing a version-control coat.

Docker

Docker image layers are content-addressed too, and the same reveals follow:

  • Why docker pull is often so fast: it skips the layers whose content hash you already have. (Caching — property 4.)
  • Why layers are shared across different images: two images built on the same base have layers with the same content, so the same hash, so they're stored once. (Dedup — property 2.)
  • Why a sha256: image digest means something: it guarantees you pulled exactly the image you meant, byte for byte, with no silent substitution. (Integrity — property 1.)

Every one of those conveniences you take for granted is the same idea quietly at work.

IPFS

IPFS makes content-addressing the entire premise, which is why it's the cleanest example. On the normal web, you fetch a file from a location — this server, that URL. On IPFS, you fetch a file by its content hash (called a CID). You're not asking "what's on this server?" — you're asking "who has the thing whose fingerprint is this?", and anyone on the network who has that content can serve it, because the same file produces the same address no matter where it lives. Location stops mattering; identity is everything.

But wait — what if two things have the same fingerprint?

If you’ve been reading closely, a question has probably been forming, and it’s the right one to ask — because the entire idea hinges on the answer.

Content-addressing assumes that no two different pieces of content ever produce the same hash. That event — two different inputs, one identical fingerprint — is called a collision, and if it could happen easily, the whole scheme would fall apart: two different files would share an address, and “same hash means same content” would become a lie.

So why do we trust it? Because with a good cryptographic hash, collisions are astronomically unlikely. Not “unlikely like winning the lottery” — unlikely like every person on Earth winning the lottery, on the same day, for a thousand years running. The space of possible hashes is so vast (for SHA-256, that’s 2²⁵⁶ values — a number larger than the count of atoms in the observable universe) that in practice you can treat “same hash = same content” as simply true, and build version control for the entire planet on top of that assumption.

But “in practice” is doing real work in that sentence, and here’s the concrete story that proves the point. Git originally used a hash called SHA-1. Over the years, SHA-1 weakened — researchers eventually managed to deliberately construct two different inputs with the same SHA-1 hash, which is exactly the collision the model depends on never happening. So git undertook a careful, years-long migration to SHA-256. Not because content-addressing was flawed, but because the whole thing rests on collisions being infeasible, and when the old hash got shaky, the one load-bearing assumption had to be shored up.

That’s the honest footnote to the beautiful idea: content-addressing is only ever as trustworthy as the hash underneath it. The elegance is real — but “which hash function” isn’t a minor detail, it’s the thing holding the entire structure up. The idea is beautiful; the hash is what makes it hold.

The takeaway

Here's the whole thing, one more time, so it sticks: if you name data by what it is instead of where it lives, you get integrity, deduplication, immutability, and caching as a free gift — which is exactly why the tools you trust most are quietly built on it.

It's a small idea with a very long reach. And now it's yours. You'll start noticing it everywhere — in a commit hash, a Docker digest, a CID, and places you haven't looked yet — and that noticing, that seeing of the idea beneath the tool, is the difference between using something and understanding it.

Fifteen minutes, one idea, and your tools make more sense than they did when you started. As promised.

Genuinely curious: what's a concept like this one for you — a single small idea you learned that suddenly explained a dozen tools at once? Content-addressing was one of mine; I remember the exact moment git stopped being magic. And now that you know git is content-addressed: what else about it just clicked into place?

articles.body_html:
Your tests pass. But would they catch a bug?

Imagine asking an AI coding agent to implement a feature. A few minutes later, it has generated the implementation, written unit tests, and opened a pull request.

The CI pipeline is green. All tests pass. Code coverage looks good.

Can you trust the change?

Not necessarily.

The implementation and its tests may share the same misunderstanding of the requirements. The tests might execute every line without checking the behavior that matters. And a test suite that passes today might not detect a regression tomorrow.

As AI makes code generation faster, we need to think more carefully about how we verify the code we produce.

In this tutorial, we'll explore one technique that can help: mutation testing.

We'll build a small TypeScript project, introduce a bug deliberately, install StrykerJS, and use mutation testing to discover weaknesses in our tests. Then we'll explore how the same technique can help us verify AI-generated pull requests.

By the end, you'll understand not just how mutation testing works, but why it can become an important part of a multi-layer verification strategy.

1. Let's start with a simple problem

Imagine we're building an online shop. One of our business rules is that orders worth £100 or more qualify for free shipping.

Let's implement that rule in TypeScript.

Create a file named src/shipping.ts:

export function calculateShipping(
  orderTotal: number,
): number {
  return orderTotal >= 100 ? 0 : 10;
}

The function is straightforward:

  • Orders below £100 pay £10 shipping.
  • Orders worth £100 or more get free shipping.

Now let's write some unit tests.

Create src/shipping.test.ts:

import { describe, expect, it } from 'vitest';
import { calculateShipping } from './shipping';

describe('calculateShipping', () => {
  it('charges shipping for small orders', () => {
    expect(calculateShipping(50)).toBe(10);
  });

  it('offers free shipping for large orders', () => {
    expect(calculateShipping(150)).toBe(0);
  });
});

Run the tests:

npx vitest run

Both tests pass.

Great! We have an implementation, some unit tests, and a green test suite.

But let's ask a slightly different question.

What would happen if somebody accidentally changed >= to >?

Our implementation would become:

export function calculateShipping(
  orderTotal: number,
): number {
  return orderTotal > 100 ? 0 : 10;
}

Now an order worth exactly £100 is charged shipping, even though the requirement says it should qualify for free shipping.

We've introduced a bug.

Run the existing tests again.

They still pass!

Why? Because we tested orders worth £50 and £150, but we never tested the boundary at £100.

Our tests execute the function, but they don't distinguish the correct implementation from this incorrect one.

This is the problem mutation testing helps us investigate.

2. What is mutation testing?

Mutation testing is a technique for evaluating how effectively your tests detect certain defects.

Instead of simply running your tests against your implementation, a mutation-testing tool deliberately makes small changes to your production code and runs the tests against each modified version.

These changes are called mutations. Each modified version is called a mutant.

For example, a mutation-testing tool might make changes such as:

Original code Mutated code
a >= b a > b
a + b a - b
isValid && isActive `isValid
{% raw %}return true return false

The tool then observes whether your tests detect the change.

There are two particularly important outcomes.

Killed mutant: At least one test fails because of the mutation. Your tests detected the change.

Survived mutant: The tests still pass. Your tests didn't detect the change.

Let's apply this to our shipping example.

The original implementation is:

return orderTotal >= 100 ? 0 : 10;

A mutant changes it to:

return orderTotal > 100 ? 0 : 10;

Our existing tests still pass, so the mutant survives.

That's a useful finding. It tells us that the test suite doesn't distinguish these two implementations.

Notice what we're evaluating: we're not simply asking whether the implementation works for our current examples. We're asking whether the tests can detect selected changes that might introduce defects.

This is a different question from ordinary unit testing and code coverage.

3. Code coverage isn't the same as test effectiveness

You may already measure code coverage in your projects.

Coverage tells you which parts of your code were executed during testing. It's useful, but it doesn't necessarily tell you whether your assertions are strong enough.

Consider this test:

it('calculates shipping', () => {
  calculateShipping(100);
});

The function executes. Depending on the coverage measurement, the test may contribute to branch or line coverage.

But the test doesn't assert the expected result.

The implementation could return £10 instead of £0, and the test would still pass.

Now consider:

it('offers free shipping at exactly £100', () => {
  expect(calculateShipping(100)).toBe(0);
});

This test checks the actual business rule.

It also kills our mutant because the mutated implementation returns £10.

We can summarize the difference:

  • Code coverage: Did our tests execute this code?
  • Assertions: Did our tests verify the expected behavior?
  • Mutation testing: Would our tests detect selected changes to the implementation?

These techniques complement each other. Mutation testing doesn't replace coverage, and a mutation score doesn't prove correctness. Together, however, they can provide more useful evidence about the effectiveness of a test suite.

4. Let's set up StrykerJS

We'll use StrykerJS, a mutation-testing framework for JavaScript and TypeScript.

We'll assume you already have Node.js and npm installed.

If you're following along from scratch, create a project:

mkdir mutation-testing-demo
cd mutation-testing-demo
npm init -y

Install TypeScript and Vitest:

npm install --save-dev typescript vitest

Create the src directory and add the two files from the previous sections.

Now run:

npx vitest run

Make sure your tests pass before continuing.

Initialize StrykerJS

Run:

npx stryker init

Follow the prompts to configure Stryker for your project. Select TypeScript and the Vitest test runner where applicable.

Stryker's setup options can vary with the version and project configuration, so follow the current prompts rather than assuming every project requires an identical configuration.

Official documentation: StrykerJS — Getting Started.

Once initialization is complete, inspect the generated configuration and make sure the mutation scope includes our production file:

src/shipping.ts

Our test file, src/shipping.test.ts, should not be treated as production code to mutate.

You can configure the mutation scope explicitly if necessary. For example, in a TypeScript Stryker configuration, the relevant pattern might be:

mutate: ['src/**/*.ts', '!src/**/*.test.ts'],

Keep the configuration generated by your installed version as the starting point, and adapt it to your repository's conventions.

Run your first mutation test

Execute:

npx stryker run

Stryker will run your tests, generate mutations in the configured production code, and evaluate the results.

The first run may take longer than your ordinary unit tests because Stryker needs to evaluate multiple mutants.

Once it finishes, inspect the terminal output and generated HTML report.

Look for surviving mutants associated with the comparison in calculateShipping.

If the comparison changes from >= to > and all our tests still pass, we've found the weakness we deliberately introduced.

Congratulations: you've just used mutation testing to discover a gap in your test suite.

5. Understand the mutation report

A mutation report contains more than just a score.

The most useful outcomes to understand are:

Killed

A test detected the mutation and failed. This is generally what we want for a meaningful behavioral change.

Survived

The tests passed despite the mutation. Investigate whether this reveals missing test coverage or an assertion that doesn't adequately verify the requirement.

No coverage

The mutated code wasn't exercised by the relevant tests. You may need to investigate whether the code is tested at all.

Timeout

The tool couldn't obtain a normal result within its configured time limit. This doesn't necessarily mean your tests detected the mutation.

Equivalent mutant

The mutation doesn't change observable behavior for the relevant inputs. No meaningful test can distinguish it from the original implementation.

Not every surviving mutant is a defect, and not every mutant needs to be killed. Some mutations are equivalent, some aren't meaningful for your requirements, and some may reveal behavior you don't actually need to constrain.

The purpose of the report is to help you make better decisions about your tests.

What about the mutation score?

Stryker calculates a mutation score based on the results of mutation testing.

A simplified formula is:

Mutation score = killed mutants / valid mutants × 100%

For example, suppose a run produces 100 valid mutants and your tests kill 80 of them. The mutation score is 80%.

That can be a useful signal, but be careful about treating it as a universal quality metric.

Two projects can have the same mutation score while having very different levels of risk. The score depends on the mutations generated, the code being analyzed, and which results are excluded.

A surviving mutation in payment authorization may matter much more than a surviving mutation in an unimportant formatting helper.

Focus on understanding meaningful surviving mutants, not maximizing a percentage at any cost.

6. Improve the tests and run mutation testing again

Let's fix the weakness we discovered.

Our business rule is explicit: orders worth £100 or more qualify for free shipping.

We should test the boundary directly.

Add this test to src/shipping.test.ts:

it('offers free shipping at exactly £100', () => {
  expect(calculateShipping(100)).toBe(0);
});

Run the ordinary test suite:

npx vitest run

The test passes against the correct implementation.

Now run mutation testing again:

npx stryker run

The mutation that changes >= to > should now be killed by the boundary test.

We've improved the test suite because it now detects a meaningful defect.

Notice that we didn't add a test just to improve a score. We added one because the requirement explicitly defines what should happen at the boundary.

This distinction is important.

A mutation-testing report is a source of questions, not an instruction to write more assertions blindly.

For every surviving mutant, ask:

  1. Does this change affect behavior that matters?
  2. What does the requirement say the correct behavior should be?
  3. Should the test suite detect this change?
  4. If so, what is the smallest meaningful test that would detect it?

This approach fits naturally into Test-Driven Development.

TDD helps us implement behavior from requirements. Mutation testing challenges whether our tests can detect selected deviations from that behavior.

7. From local experiments to pull request verification

So far, we've run mutation testing manually.

The next step is to integrate it into CI.

Imagine an AI coding agent creates a PR that modifies calculateShipping and adds several unit tests.

The ordinary CI pipeline runs:

  1. Type-checking.
  2. Linting.
  3. Unit and integration tests.
  4. Other project-specific checks.

Everything passes.

Now Stryker runs against the configured production code. It discovers that the tests don't detect a meaningful mutation in the shipping calculation.

The PR report can expose that weakness before the change is merged.

This is particularly useful for AI-generated code because the implementation and its tests may have been produced by the same agent, based on the same interpretation of the requirements.

The tests passing is evidence that the implementation satisfies the assertions the agent wrote. It isn't independent evidence that those assertions capture every important requirement.

Mutation testing adds another challenge: it deliberately changes the implementation and checks whether the test suite notices.

Should mutation testing block every PR?

I'd start with a gradual approach.

Stage 1: Report findings without blocking merges.

Run mutation testing on a small set of important modules. Learn how long it takes, inspect surviving mutants, and identify noisy or irrelevant results.

Stage 2: Gate critical code.

Introduce stronger requirements for areas where correctness is particularly important, such as permissions, pricing, validation, or state transitions.

Stage 3: Track regressions over time.

Use scheduled runs and historical reports to identify weaknesses across the broader codebase.

For larger projects, Stryker's incremental mode can reuse eligible previous results to reduce the work needed on subsequent runs. See the incremental testing documentation.

One important distinction: mutating changed production files is not the same as testing only the new tests in a PR. You want relevant existing tests to participate in verifying the changed behavior as well.

You should also avoid making a repository-wide mutation score an immediate merge requirement. A small PR shouldn't necessarily be responsible for fixing every weakness in a legacy test suite.

8. Let the AI agent investigate surviving mutants

We can take the workflow a step further.

Instead of using mutation testing only as a CI gate, we can feed its findings back to the AI agent.

Imagine this sequence:

  1. An agent implements a feature and writes unit tests.
  2. CI runs the ordinary checks.
  3. Stryker finds a surviving mutation.
  4. The agent receives the mutation report and relevant requirements.
  5. The agent determines whether the mutation exposes a genuine testing gap.
  6. The agent proposes an additional test or explains why the mutant isn't meaningful.
  7. CI reruns the checks against the revised PR.

For our shipping example, the agent might receive a report showing that changing >= to > doesn't cause any tests to fail.

The agent can then inspect the business rule and recognize that the boundary at £100 is important.

It adds the boundary test, reruns the suite, and verifies that the mutation is now killed.

This creates a feedback loop in which the agent can improve not just the implementation, but also the evidence we have about that implementation.

However, there's a critical caveat.

Don't let the agent blindly optimize the mutation score.

An agent could make a mutant fail by adding an assertion that encodes an incorrect assumption. It could also change production code simply to make the existing tests pass.

The correct behavior must come from explicit requirements, domain rules, or other trustworthy sources—not from the mutation report alone.

The agent can propose a fix, but the final verification should run independently in CI against the revised commit.

9. Mutation testing is one layer in a Swiss cheese model

This brings us to the broader reason mutation testing matters.

No single verification technique catches every defect.

Type checking can detect certain classes of errors, but it doesn't establish that a business rule is correct.

Unit tests can verify specified behavior, but they only check the cases and assertions we've written.

Mutation testing can challenge the effectiveness of those tests, but it can't guarantee that the original requirements were understood correctly.

Integration tests can expose problems between components, but they won't necessarily identify every defect in an individual component.

Code review can identify design and requirement problems, but human reviewers also have limited time and attention.

Each layer has gaps.

This is the idea behind a Swiss cheese model of verification: arrange multiple imperfect defenses so that a defect that passes through one layer has other opportunities to be detected.

A practical model might include:

Layer 1: Types and static analysis

Catch incompatible interfaces, invalid types, and selected classes of programming mistakes.

Layer 2: Unit and integration tests

Check specified behavior, interactions, and component integration.

Layer 3: Mutation testing

Challenge whether tests detect selected changes to the implementation.

Layer 4: Contract and architecture checks

Verify boundaries, invariants, and integration assumptions.

Layer 5: Independent review and production feedback

Identify misunderstood requirements, broader design risks, and failures that automated checks miss.

The layers are complementary. They aren't completely independent: mutation testing relies on the test suite, and both can be based on the same misunderstood requirement.

But combining different forms of verification can provide stronger evidence than relying on any one of them.

This connects directly to the principles discussed in Revisiting the Toyota Production System in the Age of Coding Agents. In particular, the idea of building quality into the production process is relevant here: detect abnormalities as early as possible, rather than allowing them to move downstream.

Mutation testing can be one of the automated checks that helps us detect weaknesses before a pull request is merged.

10. Why this matters when code generation scales

AI changes the economics of software development.

An agent can produce a substantial implementation and its accompanying tests much faster than a human might write them manually.

But generating code is not the same as establishing that the code is correct.

If the volume of changes increases dramatically, manually reviewing every implementation and every test may become increasingly difficult.

We need verification mechanisms that scale with the rate of change.

This is the connection to When Code Gets Cheap, Verification Becomes Expensive.

Mutation testing is not a complete solution to that problem. It has a computational cost, and it only evaluates the mutations it generates. It cannot establish that the implementation satisfies every requirement or that every important defect is represented by a mutation.

What it can do is make one important question cheaper to investigate:

Can our tests detect plausible defects in the code we're producing?

And because the process can be automated, we can apply that challenge repeatedly as code changes.

The objective isn't to maximize code generation or mutation scores in isolation. It's to increase our ability to produce and verify valuable changes without letting the volume of generated code overwhelm our verification capacity.

Conclusion

Mutation testing is a relatively simple idea with important consequences.

We deliberately modify production code, run our tests, and observe whether those tests detect the changes. When meaningful mutants survive, we investigate whether our tests are missing important behavioral checks.

With TypeScript and StrykerJS, it's possible to introduce this technique into an existing project without replacing your test runner or abandoning your current TDD workflow.

And when AI agents generate code and tests, mutation testing provides a useful additional challenge: rather than accepting a green test suite at face value, we can investigate whether it detects selected mistakes.

It doesn't prove that our code is correct. No single testing technique does.

But that's precisely why it belongs in a multi-layer verification strategy.

When code generation scales, verification must scale with it. Mutation testing helps us challenge one of the most important defenses we already have: our tests.

Further reading

  • From Rigidity to Explicitness: How AI Changes the Role of Constraints in Software
  • When Code Gets Cheap, Verification Becomes Expensive
  • Revisiting the Toyota Production System in the Age of Coding Agents
  • StrykerJS documentation
