  status: "TODO" | "IN_PROGRESS" | "DONE";
  assigneeId: string;
}

const mockTasks: Task[] = [
  { id: "task_1", orgId: "org_engineering", title: "Write API documentation", status: "IN_PROGRESS", assigneeId: "usr_alex_101" },
  { id: "task_2", orgId: "org_engineering", title: "Set up CI/CD pipeline", status: "TODO", assigneeId: "usr_alex_101" },
];

export function createTaskPulseServer(options?: { authInfo?: AuthInfo }): McpServer {
  const server = new McpServer({
    name: "TaskPulse",
    version: "1.0.0",
  });

  const currentUser = options?.authInfo?.extra?.userId as string || "anonymous";
  const userOrg = options?.authInfo?.extra?.orgId as string || "default_org";
  const scopes = options?.authInfo?.scopes || [];

  // ==========================================
  // 1. TOOLS ("Do something")
  // ==========================================

  // TOOL: List Tasks (Scoped to user's organization)
  server.tool(
    "list_my_tasks",
    "List all tasks assigned to the current user in their organization.",
    {
      status: z.enum(["ALL", "TODO", "IN_PROGRESS", "DONE"]).default("ALL").optional(),
    },
    async (args) => {
      if (!scopes.includes("tasks:read")) {
        return { content: [{ type: "text", text: "Forbidden: Missing 'tasks:read' scope" }], isError: true };
      }

      const tasks = mockTasks.filter(t => t.orgId === userOrg && t.assigneeId === currentUser);
      const filtered = args.status && args.status !== "ALL" ? tasks.filter(t => t.status === args.status) : tasks;

      return {
        content: [{ type: "text", text: JSON.stringify(filtered, null, 2) }],
      };
    }
  );

  // TOOL: Create Task (Requires 'tasks:write' scope)
  server.tool(
    "create_task",
    "Create a new task in the current user's workspace.",
    {
      title: z.string().min(3).describe("Task title"),
      status: z.enum(["TODO", "IN_PROGRESS"]).default("TODO").optional(),
    },
    async (args) => {
      if (!scopes.includes("tasks:write")) {
        return { content: [{ type: "text", text: "Forbidden: Missing 'tasks:write' scope" }], isError: true };
      }

      const newTask: Task = {
        id: `task_${Date.now()}`,
        orgId: userOrg,
        title: args.title,
        status: args.status || "TODO",
        assigneeId: currentUser,
      };
      mockTasks.push(newTask);

      return {
        content: [{
          type: "text",
          text: JSON.stringify({
            success: true,
            message: `Task created successfully by ${currentUser}`,
            task: newTask,
          }, null, 2)
        }],
      };
    }
  );

  // ==========================================
  // 2. RESOURCES ("Read context")
  // ==========================================

  // Dynamic Resource: Read project details
  server.resource(
    "project-details",
    new ResourceTemplate("taskpulse://projects/{projectId}", { list: undefined }),
    async (uri, { projectId }) => {
      const pid = Array.isArray(projectId) ? projectId[0] : projectId;
      return {
        contents: [{
          uri: uri.href,
          mimeType: "application/json",
          text: JSON.stringify({
            projectId: pid,
            organization: userOrg,
            lead: currentUser,
            description: "Core sprint engineering workspace.",
          }, null, 2),
        }],
      };
    }
  );

  // ==========================================
  // 3. PROMPTS ("Guide the conversation")
  // ==========================================

  // Prompt: Generate standup update based on tasks
  server.prompt(
    "sprint_standup_summary",
    "Generate a structured daily standup report for the current user's active tasks.",
    {
      includeBlockers: z.string().optional().describe("Ask if there are any blockers (yes/no)"),
    },
    (args) => ({
      messages: [{
        role: "user",
        content: {
          type: "text",
          text: `You are my agile project assistant. Look at my assigned tasks in TaskPulse for user ${currentUser} and write a concise 3-bullet standup summary:
1. What I completed yesterday
2. What I'm working on today
3. Blockers (${args.includeBlockers || "none declared"}).`,
        },
      }],
    })
  );

  return server;
}

11. Testing Your Server (Locally & in Claude/Cursor)

1. Run the Server 

# In your terminal
npm run build && node --max-http-header-size=65536 dist/index.js

2. Configure Claude Desktop

Open your configuration file:

  • macOS: ~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json
  • Windows: %APPDATA%\Claude\claude_desktop_config.json

Add your remote server:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "taskpulse": {
      "url": "http://localhost:8080/sse"
    }
  }
}

3. Watch the Magic Happen

  1. Start Claude Desktop.
  2. Claude hits http://localhost:8080/sse and receives the 401 Unauthorized with the Protected Resource header.
  3. Claude automatically opens your browser to: http://localhost:8080/authorize?client_id=claude-desktop&...
  4. You see your dark-mode TaskPulse consent screen!
  5. Enter alex@example.com and password correct-horse-battery, then click Authorize Access.
  6. The browser redirects to http://localhost/callback?code=....
  7. Claude exchanges the code for the JWT token and connects to the SSE stream.
  8. Ask Claude: > "What tasks are assigned to me in TaskPulse?" > Claude calls list_my_tasks and replies with your tasks! >

12. Production Gotchas & Best Practices

Here are four lessons we learned the hard way when deploying MCP servers:

1. Node.js Header Size Limit

  • The Issue: With OAuth JWTs, cookies, and CORS headers, requests can exceed Node's default header limit (8KB-16KB) and throw 431 Request Header Fields Too Large.
  • The Fix: Always start Node with --max-http-header-size=65536.

2. The Issuer URL in Cloud Deployments

  • The Issue: If your server issues tokens with iss: "http://localhost:8080", but your production server lives at https://mcp.yourdomain.com, token verification will fail.
  • The Fix: Dynamically set the issuerUrl using an environment variable (APP_URL): 
  const issuerUrl = new URL(process.env.APP_URL || `http://localhost:${PORT}`);

3. Store Tokens in Redis / Database in Production

  • In this tutorial, we used in-memory Maps for sessions and tokens.
  • In production, if your cloud provider restarts your container or runs multiple replicas, in-memory tokens will be lost. Store your authorization codes and refresh tokens in Redis or PostgreSQL.

4. Always Enforce Scope Verification Inside Tools

  • Don't just check if a user is logged in. Check what they are allowed to do! Check scopes.includes("tasks:write") before mutating data.

Happy building!

articles.title: You Installed a Library for Numbers PerformanceObserver Already Has.
articles.description: The web-vitals npm package gets credit for data your browser already computes. Here's what three PerformanceObserver calls give you for free — and the one piece of math it quietly saves you from getting wrong.
articles.body_html:
Your bundle analyzer flags a new dependency after a routine npm install. Two kilobytes, not huge, but you go looking anyway. It's web-vitals — the package half the performance tutorials on the internet tell you to install just so you can console.log three numbers: LCP, CLS, INP.

You open its source expecting something clever. It's mostly PerformanceObserver calls. The exact same API already sitting in your browser, for free, before your bundle even finishes downloading.

So why does nearly everyone reach for the library first? There's exactly one part of this that's genuinely hard to get right by hand — and it's not the part most people worry about.

Measuring LCP by hand takes four lines

Largest Contentful Paint is the easy one. The browser already tracks which element painted the biggest visible chunk of content, and it hands you updates as a better candidate shows up:

new PerformanceObserver((list) => {
  const entries = list.getEntries();
  const lastEntry = entries[entries.length - 1];
  console.log("LCP so far:", lastEntry.startTime, lastEntry.element);
}).observe({ type: "largest-contentful-paint", buffered: true });

buffered: true is the part people forget and then can't figure out why their observer logs nothing — it backfills entries that happened before this script ran, which for LCP is usually all of them, since your analytics script rarely loads before the hero image paints.

The browser keeps revising "largest so far" as bigger elements paint in, and stops for good the moment the user scrolls, clicks, or types, or the tab goes hidden — at that point, whatever the last entry said is the final score. entry.element is the actual DOM node, which is a nice touch for debugging ("oh, the LCP element is the hidden carousel slide, not the headline") — except when it's null, which happens if the element has already been removed from the DOM by the time your callback runs. (A separate gotcha hits cross-origin images without a Timing-Allow-Origin header: element still resolves, but renderTime reads as 0, so you have to fall back to loadTime instead — a different field going quiet, not the element.)

Four lines, one footgun, done. This is not the part web-vitals is earning its keep on.

Where the naive version lies to you: CLS

Cumulative Layout Shift reports as a layout-shift entry every time something visible moves without the user asking it to. Each entry has a .value — how much of the viewport shifted, weighted by distance. The obvious thing to do is sum them:

let clsTotal = 0;
new PerformanceObserver((list) => {
  for (const entry of list.getEntries()) {
    if (!entry.hadRecentInput) clsTotal += entry.value;
  }
  console.log("CLS so far:", clsTotal);
}).observe({ type: "layout-shift", buffered: true });

(hadRecentInput is true if the shift happened within 500ms of the user clicking or typing — an accordion that resizes after you click it shouldn't count against you, so the spec excludes it.)

Ship that on a dashboard that stays open all day, with an ad slot that occasionally reflows, and watch clsTotal climb to 3, then 6, then double digits by the afternoon. Nothing on the page ever visibly jumped badly — a few small shifts, hours apart. The number is technically "correct" by your own code, and it is nowhere close to what the real metric reports, because real CLS was never meant to be a lifetime total.

Before you scroll: what do you think the actual rule is? A cap? A time window? A per-minute budget?

It's a session window. Group shifts where the gap since the last one is under 1 second, cap each group at 5 seconds total, and report whichever single window ever added up to the most:

let windows = [];
let current = null;

new PerformanceObserver((list) => {
  for (const entry of list.getEntries()) {
    if (entry.hadRecentInput) continue;

    const since = entry.startTime - (current?.last ?? -Infinity);
    const span = entry.startTime - (current?.start ?? entry.startTime);

    if (current && since < 1000 && span < 5000) {
      current.sum += entry.value;
      current.last = entry.startTime;
    } else {
      current = { start: entry.startTime, last: entry.startTime, sum: entry.value };
      windows.push(current);
    }
  }
  const cls = Math.max(0, ...windows.map((w) => w.sum));
  console.log("CLS (session-windowed):", cls);
}).observe({ type: "layout-shift", buffered: true });

A burst of shifts from one bad ad reflow — all within a second or two of each other — stays grouped into one window and still hurts your score, correctly. But five unrelated shifts scattered across an afternoon never combine into one number, because they never do to a real visitor either: nobody experiences "all the jank from today," they experience one moment where the page jumped under their thumb.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

INP has the same trap, with an extra twist

The naive move for Interaction to Next Paint is to listen for event entries and log every duration:

new PerformanceObserver((list) => {
  for (const entry of list.getEntries()) {
    console.log(entry.name, entry.duration);
  }
}).observe({ type: "event", buffered: true, durationThreshold: 16 });

Tap a button on a touchscreen and this fires three or four times — pointerdown, pointerup, click, sometimes more — for what the user experienced as one tap. Log each duration as its own interaction and you've just told your dashboard there were four slow interactions where there was one.

The fix is grouping: every event entry belonging to the same physical interaction shares an interactionId, so you group by that and take the worst duration inside each group — one number per real interaction, not one per DOM event:

const interactions = new Map();

new PerformanceObserver((list) => {
  for (const entry of list.getEntries()) {
    if (!entry.interactionId) continue; // 0 means "not a tracked interaction"
    const existing = interactions.get(entry.interactionId) ?? 0;
    interactions.set(entry.interactionId, Math.max(existing, entry.duration));
  }
}).observe({ type: "event", buffered: true, durationThreshold: 16 });

Even that map isn't the final INP score — the real metric doesn't just report Math.max(...interactions.values()) either. A single freak slow tap (a GC pause at the wrong millisecond) shouldn't define the whole page's score any more than one slow HTTP request should define your p50 latency. The reference implementation tracks a high percentile across the session instead of the single worst value once there have been enough interactions to make a percentile meaningful — which is a few lines of arithmetic you do not want to be debugging for the first time during an incident.

So what is the library actually for?

Not the measuring — you just watched that happen in nine lines. It's the three things nobody gets right the first time they hand-roll this: the CLS session-windowing, the INP interaction-grouping-plus-percentile, and the edge cases around bfcache restores and visibility-change timing that silently double-report or under-report a metric if you don't special-case them. That's real, fiddly logic, and web-vitals has had years of bug reports to get it right. If you're sending these numbers to a real-user-monitoring pipeline that someone makes decisions from, use the library for exactly that math.

Here's the honest caveat, and it's narrower than it would have been a year ago: Safari was the last of the three engines to ship largest-contentful-paint and interaction-level event timing (the interactionId grouping above), adding both in Safari 26.2, December 2025. Firefox isn't new to this — it's had largest-contentful-paint since version 122 (early 2024) — but it only picked up interactionId around the same time as Safari, in Firefox 144. With Safari's December 2025 release, all three engines finally agreed on both entry types, which is what pushed web.dev to mark LCP and INP "Baseline: Newly available" at that point. layout-shift didn't make the trip — Cumulative Layout Shift is still Chromium-only; Firefox's tracking bug for it has sat open since 2021, and Safari 26.2 shipped the other two without it. So CLS is the one metric where neither the raw API nor web-vitals can produce a number for a Firefox or Safari visitor — the library's job there is still correctness on the browsers that do report it, not conjuring data from the one that doesn't. Feature-detect before you rely on any of this:

if (PerformanceObserver.supportedEntryTypes.includes("layout-shift")) {
  // measure it
} else {
  // this visitor is on a browser that can't tell you
}

🧠 Test yourself

Think it clicked? Take the 7-question quiz →

Instant feedback, a hint on every question, and an explanation for each answer — right or wrong.

The library isn't buying you the measurement — the browser was always going to hand you that, Chromium or nothing. It's buying you the arithmetic that's easy to get wrong exactly once, in production, where you won't notice until the dashboard looks wrong for a month. Have you ever shipped a CLS or INP number you'd now bet was quietly miscounted? I'd genuinely like to know in the comments.

  • Shadow DOM Needed JavaScript to Exist. Now It Doesn't.

articles.title: What AI crawlers are blind to: the text your JavaScript renders
articles.description: I run a small property site. Four languages, plain HTML, no framework, no npm dependencies, hosted on...
articles.body_html:
I run a small property site. Four languages, plain HTML, no framework, no npm dependencies, hosted on Cloudflare Pages. I have spent my working life on copy and search, so I did the usual things: structured data, hreflang, a sitemap, a generator that keeps every page's head in sync from one file.

Then I ran one command against my own listing page:

curl -s -A 'GPTBot/1.0' https://example.com/my-listing | \
  python3 -c "import sys,re,html; b=sys.stdin.read(); b=b[b.index('<body'):]; \
  b=re.sub(r'<script.*?</script>','',b,flags=re.S); \
  print(len(re.sub(r'\s+',' ',html.unescape(re.sub(r'<[^>]+>',' ',b))).strip()))"

It counts the visible text in <body> after removing scripts. That is roughly what a crawler gets if it does not execute JavaScript.

The answer for my listing page was 23 characters. For my homepage, 17.

Where the text had gone

Nowhere surprising, once you look. The site is multilingual, and the copy for every language lives in assets/js/i18n.js. On load, app.js picks the language and fills the containers:

var descEl = document.querySelector("[data-listing-description]");
if (descEl) descEl.innerHTML = l.description + climateNoteFor(id);

That is a perfectly ordinary pattern. It also means the HTML I ship contains the layout and nothing to read.

Googlebot renders JavaScript, so Google was fine. The question is everyone else.

What the crawler did get

Not nothing. The head carried 2,891 characters of JSON-LD: name, price, number of rooms, floor area, address, coordinates, amenities. A machine could reconstruct a tidy product card from that.

And that is exactly what made it worse.

My site exists for one reason: it is a private sale, direct from the owner, and every listing states plainly what the title deed situation is — the kind of sentence an agency leaves out. That sentence lives in the prose. So a crawler without JavaScript got the price and the square metres, identical to any agency listing, and none of the disclosure the site was built around. The one thing that made the page different was the one thing it could not read.

Why no dashboard told me

Analytics did not show this, and could not. My analytics runs on JavaScript. It counts visitors whose browsers execute scripts, which by definition excludes every client that does not. The blind spot is the measurement instrument, not the site.

What did show it was Cloudflare's AI crawler log. In 24 hours up to 15 September 2026 my domain took 43 requests from AI crawlers: Applebot 20, Googlebot 14, Meta-ExternalAgent 8, GPTBot 1. They fetched pages, the sitemap, images, the CSS, both JS files, and the favicon I had published an hour earlier.

Worth noting, since it is the fashionable question: llms.txt sits in my site root, and across 23 distinct crawled paths in that window it was requested exactly zero times. Cloudflare's own readiness checklist did not mention the file either. On that day its items were robots.txt, a sitemap, content signals, markdown versions of pages, and WebMCP.

The fix, and why it was cheap

I already had a generator for the head. It takes one data file and writes it into every page between markers:

<!-- SEO:START (generated by build/generate-seo.js — do not hand-edit between markers) -->
...
<!-- SEO:END -->

The previous post is about it. The same idea works for the body. I put markers inside the containers the script already fills:

<div class="listing-description" data-listing-description><!-- BODY:listing-description --><!-- /BODY:listing-description --></div>

and taught the generator to fill them from i18n.js and listings-data.js — the same files the browser uses. That detail is the whole point: the static text cannot drift from what the script renders, because there is one source and one build step. app.js still redraws those containers on load, so the language switcher behaves exactly as before.

Results, same command as above:

Page Before After (15 September 2026)
Homepage 17 2,648
Listing 23 3,127
About 17 995

Total work: one script and a pass that inserted markers. No framework, no SSR runtime, no rewrite.

What I would take from this

A generator earns its keep twice. The first time when it saves you from editing twenty files by hand. The second time when a new requirement lands and the data is already in one place, so the fix is a function rather than a project.

And the general version, which is older than any of this: check what the machine receives, not what your browser draws. The page looked finished in every browser I opened. It was empty to anything that did not run my JavaScript, and it stayed that way for weeks because every tool I used to check it ran JavaScript too.

Run the command above on your own site. It takes ten seconds. If your stack renders on the server you will see a number in the thousands and can stop reading. If you see two digits, you now know something your analytics will never tell you.

The site: https://girne-apartment-sale.com/?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=article04

Standalone, genericized version of the generator, if you want the code rather than the description: https://github.com/sergei-swh/seo-generator

articles.title: How I’m Building Modi: An AI-Powered Learning Assistant as a Student Developer
articles.description: I’m a Student Developer Building an AI Learning Assistant Called Modi   I've always been...
articles.body_html:
I’m a Student Developer Building an AI Learning Assistant Called Modi

I've always been interested in technology, but I didn't want to spend all my time just learning about what other people were building. I wanted to build something of my own.

That is one of the reasons I started working on Modi, an AI-powered learning assistant within my project, Modupath.

I'm still a student, and I'm still learning. But I wanted to see what I could create if I took an idea seriously and kept working on it.

Where the Idea Came From

One thing that made me think differently about learning technology was how difficult it can be for students to get access to AI tools in some learning environments.

I started thinking about what a learning assistant designed with students in mind could look like.

That idea became Modi.

I didn't want it to be just another website with a chat box. I wanted to build something that could bring different learning tools together and give students a useful place to work.

Of course, having an idea is one thing. Actually building it is another.

Building It Has Taught Me a Lot

Working on Modi has taken me beyond simply designing a webpage.

I've worked with JavaScript, Node.js, Firebase, and AI APIs. I've also spent time connecting different parts of the application and working through the problems that come with making software function properly.

For example, an AI response appearing on a screen is only one part of the experience. There's also the work behind user authentication, saving information, connecting the frontend to the backend, and making sure things work as expected.

I've had to learn that a feature isn't really finished just because it looks good. It needs to work, too.

And when something doesn't work, you have to investigate it, test possible solutions, and keep learning.

I'm still improving Modi, so this is an ongoing process rather than a finished success story.

Why I'm Sharing This

I created this post because I want to start sharing more of what I build and learn.

Sometimes, when you see software developers online, you mostly see the finished product. You don't always see the learning, debugging, experiments, and changes that happen along the way.

I want to share more of that process.

I'm particularly interested in web development, artificial intelligence, and how technology can make learning more useful for students.

I also want to learn from developers who have more experience than I do. There is still a lot I don't know, and I'm fine with that. The important thing is to keep improving.

What's Next for Modi?

I want to keep improving the application, make the experience more useful, and learn from feedback.

I'm also working on becoming a better developer, not just building more features. That means paying attention to how software is designed, how it works behind the scenes, and how people actually use it.

If you're interested in seeing what I'm working on, here are a few links:

  • My portfolio: https://software-portfolio-five-pi.vercel.app/

I'm sharing this as the beginning of my journey on DEV, and I hope to share more practical lessons as I continue building.

If you're a developer, especially someone who's still learning, what's one thing building your own project has taught you that tutorials never did?
